blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($Δd' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.
blocks.zh: 培训后是否改变语文模式代表什么,或如何将这种表述理解为答案? 我们比较了线性探测器 和模型本身的答案, 用信号检测理论分析, 在6个开放量级基模型 及其训练后的版本。 对于判断德文文本是由人类还是由AI编写,探针和n-gm分类词将各类区分得很好,但答案没有而且常常是反向命令文本. 培训后平均降低了答案的敏感性(模范家庭的“Δd'=-0.34美元;3个提示的0.29)。 它还改变了说明的基准率的使用: 基础模型转换了它们的对数,比之前的概率变化小,大多数经过培训后模型变化更多。 在设有阶段性检查站的两个模式中,变化发生在监督的微调期间,模型缝合影响到了早期的层次,并且从中深入到文本之后的各国内部位置,而不是文本中的位置,转移了检查站之间的变化。 我们的公司不能共享,所以我们增加一个可以从公共数据中复制的案件,即否定声明的真相. 在这方面,培训后的行动方向相反: 探测器在每个模型中解码出或接近天花板的真相,数个基模型的答案没有使用,训练后修复;通过中深度的修复,在陈述后停留在位置上;下面是陈述的表述,在四个模型中的一个中有很大的贡献. 在一项培训研究中,在原本相同的微调数据中,加上2000个正确标注的作者对新闻文本的判断,改进了我们报纸和教科书Corpora的答案,并在聊天中倒置了答案,他们在谈话中遵循了经过新闻训练的对基模型的探针. 因此,后培训改变了判断如何从模型中表达出来,一个小型的培训信号可以确定其方向。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
What does post-training change in a language model? After pretraining on
large text corpora, language models are turned into assistants in
several stages of post-training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), in which
the model learns to imitate example dialogues, and stages that optimize
it for human or AI preferences, e.g., direct preference optimization
(DPO), in which it learns to prefer the better of two candidate answers.
An influential view holds that these stages add little knowledge: A
model learns what it knows during pretraining, and post-training mainly
teaches it in which format and style to respond. Zhou et al.
( 2023 ) formulated this as the
superficial alignment hypothesis, and several findings are consistent
with it, among them that a few well-chosen examples or a suitable prompt
to a base model can produce much of the behavior of a fully post-trained
model (Lin et al., 2023 ), and that
instructions change how a model expresses information more than how it
encodes it (Waldis et al., 2026 ). If this view is
correct, post-training should leave a model’s internal representations
largely intact while changing how they are read out into an answer. This
distinction matters beyond its theoretical interest: A model whose
answers no longer reflect what it represents knows something but says
something else, which is a central concern for assessing the honesty of
language models. Testing the distinction, however, requires a judgment
for which we know what the model should represent, can measure whether
it does, and can pinpoint where the representation diverges from the
answer.

blocks.en:
We argue that judging the authorship of a text, i.e., whether it was
written by a human or generated by an AI, is such a test case, for
several reasons. The correct answer is known for every text, so that
both the model’s representation and its answer can be scored against the
same ground truth. Authorship is a property of the input text, which the
model reads in full before it answers; the information is therefore
available in principle and does not depend on retrieving facts from
memory. Whether the distinguishing information is present can be
established independently of the model, with simple text statistics.
Texts can be chosen that the models are unlikely to have seen, or cannot
have seen, during training, which rules out memorization. Humans make
the same judgment, which connects the question to a long tradition of
research on human judgment. The judgment is also of practical relevance,
because AI-generated text has become hard to tell apart from human
writing in education, journalism, and science, human readers perform
close to chance (Clark et al., 2021 ; Jakesch et al., 2023 ; Jones & Bergen, 2025 ; Köbis & Mossink, 2021 ; Porter & Machery, 2024 ), and detectors trained
specifically for this purpose are in wide use (Thai et al., 2025 ). Human judgments rely on
plausible but invalid heuristics, such as taking references to personal
experience or first-person pronouns as signs of human authorship
(Jakesch et al., 2023 ), and
only readers who frequently use language models for their own writing
appear to detect AI-generated text reliably (Russell et al., 2025 ). Because the texts
that make authorship a clean test case cannot be shared, we complement
it with a second judgment on public data that meets the same
requirements and can be reproduced in full: whether a statement is true,
for statements with and without negation (Marks & Tegmark, 2024 ).

blocks.en:
One might expect language models to do better. They produce such texts
themselves, and the regularities that distinguish their output from
human writing are, in principle, available to them. However, language
models asked directly whether a text was written by a human or by an AI
are weak and biased judges: Their errors lean in one direction, and the
direction differs between models and model generations (Bhattacharjee &
Liu, 2024 ; Yuan et
al., 2026 ). When GPT-3.5 and
GPT-4 judged transcripts of Turing-test conversations, their accuracy
was even below chance (Rathi et al., 2024 ). In pilot work with the
German chat messages used here, four commercial models judged each
message with five prompt versions and rated their confidence. Two of
them, GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6, had written the AI messages
themselves. None of the four models recognized these messages: With any
prompt version, each model called at most 16% of them AI, and the two
generators called at most 7% and 14% of their own messages AI. The
confidence ratings ordered the messages below chance in the smallest
model (GPT-5.4-mini: AUC = .20–.34) and at or above chance in the
larger ones (GPT-5.4: .53–.73; Claude Sonnet 4.6: .63–.76; Claude Opus
4.6: .69–.90). Why would a model that writes like an AI fail to
recognize AI-written text, and why would the training that makes it a
helpful assistant make it worse at this?

blocks.en:
Two classic frameworks from psychology are helpful in asking this
question precisely. Signal detection theory separates the sensitivity of
a judge, i.e., the ability to distinguish signal from noise, from the
criterion, i.e., the tendency to give one answer rather than the other
(Macmillan & Creelman, 2004 ). A bias toward
answering “human” only shifts the criterion for all texts alike; it
cannot make the evidence for “AI” stronger for human than for AI
texts. Sensitivity below chance therefore indicates that the evidence on
which the judgment is based is ordered inversely. Brunswik’s lens model
adds the distinction between the validity of the cues that a stimulus
offers and the way in which a judge utilizes them (Brunswik, 1956 ; Karelaia &
Hogarth, 2008 ). Poor judgments
can result from a lack of valid cues or from valid cues that are not
used, or used in the wrong way. For human judges, the utilization of
cues can only be inferred from their judgments. For language models, it
can be examined directly, because their internal representations are
accessible. The judgment of a language model can then be described by
two lenses in series (Figure 1): In a first lens, the cues of the text
are encoded in the model’s internal representation; in a second lens,
this representation is read out into an answer to the question.
Splitting the judge side of the lens model in this way has precedents in
research on personality judgment, which distinguishes the detection of
cues from their utilization (Funder, 1995 ), and in neuroscience,
which distinguishes the information that a neural population encodes
from the information that is read out for behavior (Panzeri et al., 2017 ). Because psychology
and machine learning often use different words for the same idea, and
sometimes the same word for different ideas, Appendix A lists the
correspondences between their terms.

blocks.en:
Figure 1: Figure 1. Brunswik’s lens model, applied to a language
model as judge and extended by an internal lens. A state of the world
(Brunswik’s distal criterion; the ground truth, here whether a text was
written by an AI, whether a statement is true, or whether a review is
genuine) is reflected in observable cues of the text, some of which are
valid and some of which are not (dashed). In the first lens (encoding),
the model integrates these cues into its internal representation;
whether the ground truth can be decoded from this representation is
measured with linear probes, and whether two checkpoints represent it in
the same way with probe transfer. In the second lens (readout), the
representation is read out into an answer to the question by weighting
internal features. Only one of these features was measured directly: the
class direction, i.e., the direction that separates the two classes in
the representation; its relation to the answer was examined with
steering at the answer position (Appendix D). The other features are
schematic. Achievement, i.e., the agreement of the answer with the state
of the world, requires both lenses. Post-training changes mainly the
second lens (orange), and in several cases also the first (Sections 3.4
and 3.6); model stitching and activation patching locate the change in
depth and in the prompt. Splitting the judge side of the lens model has
precedents in personality judgment (detection vs. utilization of cues;
Funder, 1995 ) and in
neuroscience (information encoded in a neural population vs. read out
for behavior; Panzeri et al., 2017 ). Note: for the
authorship corpora, probes were fitted both on the text positions and on
the last prompt position; for the truth and review sets, only on the
last prompt position.

blocks.en:
A brief description of how a language model processes a prompt may be
helpful for readers from psychology. The prompt is split into a sequence
of tokens (words or parts of words), and in each of its several dozen
layers the model computes an internal state for every position of this
sequence. Through the attention mechanism, the state at a position can
draw on the states at all earlier positions, but not on later ones. The
answer is generated from the state at the last position after the final
layer. In a prompt that presents a text and then asks a question about
it, information about the text can therefore reach the answer only
through the positions that follow the text, i.e., those of the question
and of the cue for the answer (Figure 2A). We refer to these parts of
the prompt as the text positions, the question positions, and the last
position. All analyses and interventions reported below are carried out
on these internal states of an artificial neural network, i.e., of a
computer program whose every state can be recorded, replaced, and
restored.

blocks.en:
Figure 2: Figure 2. How the interventions work. In panels A, C,
and D, the horizontal axis shows the positions of the prompt in reading
order (the instruction, the text to be judged, the question, and the
position at which the answer is produced), and the vertical axis shows
the layers of the network. (A) Information flow: through attention,
later positions read information from earlier ones. The answer is
produced at the last position. Information from the text reaches it
through the positions after the text: the question (dark tiles) and the
last position itself, which also reads the text directly at every layer
(the schematic shows only the route via the question). (B) Steering,
sketched in a two-dimensional version of the high-dimensional
representation space: human texts (open circles) and AI texts
(triangles) differ along an AI–human direction (arrow between the class
means). Steering moves the state of one text along this direction
(diamonds) and measures how the model’s answer changes; the dashed line
marks where the answer switches. The two need not be orthogonal: the
angle between the AI–human direction and the model’s decision boundary
determines how strongly a shift along the direction changes the answer.
If the model read the direction correctly, a shift toward the AI texts
would move the answer toward “KI”. (C) Model stitching combines the
lower layers of one checkpoint (here the base model, blue) with the
upper layers of another (here the SFT model, orange). (D) Activation
patching replaces the internal states of one model (here SFT) at
selected positions and one layer with those of the other model (here the
base model’s states at the question positions).

blocks.en:
This possibility has been used to show that language models often
represent more than they say. Simple linear classifiers (“probes”)
trained on a model’s internal activations can recover properties such as
the truth of a statement (Burns et al., 2024 ; Hu & Levy, 2023 ; Marks & Tegmark, 2024 ) or the correctness of
the model’s own answers (Orgad et al., 2025 ) better than the model’s
answers do, and prompting a model for a judgment can underestimate what
it knows (Hu & Levy, 2023 ).
The same dissociation has been reported for authorship: Models encode
whether they wrote a text themselves although they fail to report it (Y.
Zhou et al., 2026 ), and a
direction in the residual stream that tracks self-authorship can be used
to steer what a model claims to have written (Ackerman & Panickssery, 2025 ; see also
Panickssery et al., 2024 ).
Interpretability research at the scale of frontier models has made the
same distinction between the presence of a feature and the behavior it
supports (Templeton et al., 2024 ), and has identified
a small subspace of representations that a model is able to verbalize,
whose content is shaped by post-training (Gurnee et al., 2026 ). Why represented
information fails to reach the answer is less clear. One recent account
attributes such gaps to a miscalibrated decision threshold (Villuri et
al., 2026 ), i.e., to the
criterion in terms of signal detection theory, which cannot explain
sensitivity below chance. Another line of work shows that steering along
a direction that discriminates a concept can promote the opposite
behavior (Torop et al., 2026 ), which suggests that
the readout of represented information can itself be reversed.

blocks.en:
What post-training does to this relation has been studied mainly by
comparing base and post-trained models. Representations learned during
pretraining largely transfer to the post-trained model (Kissane et al., 2024 ), fine-tuning tends
to enhance existing mechanisms rather than to create new ones (Prakash
et al., 2024 ). Model
diffing, i.e., the systematic comparison of the internal representations
of a base model and its post-trained version, has been carried out with
crosscoders, sparse dictionaries of features that are learned from both
models at once and reveal which features are shared and which are
specific to one of them (Lindsey et al., 2024 ). It suggests that
much of what chat fine-tuning adds is concentrated at the tokens of the
chat template (Minder et al., 2026 ; see also Leong et
al., 2025 ), i.e., the special
tokens that mark the beginning and the end of the user’s and the
assistant’s turns and that, in a prompt, lie between the user’s text and
the answer. Likewise, exchanging the key-value cache, i.e., the stored
internal states of earlier positions that later positions read, between
fine-tuned and base models transfers fine-tuned behaviors mainly through
system-prompt and template positions (Loos & Eberle, 2026 ), and crossing the
lower and upper layers of base and post-trained models has shown that
changes in the late layers can depend on altered earlier computation (Y.
Zhou, 2026 ). For example,
the representation of whether a model is being evaluated, tracked across
the published checkpoints of one model, is already present in the base
model and amplified during supervised fine-tuning (Heidari et al., 2026 ). To our
knowledge, however, these approaches have not been combined to ask, for
a judgment with known ground truth, whether post-training changes the
representation of a property or the way in which the answer reads it
out, and where in the network this happens. Models whose developers
released checkpoints after every stage of post-training make this
possible. Combining the lower layers of one checkpoint with the upper
layers of another, a technique known as model stitching (Bansal et al., 2021 ; Lenc & Vedaldi, 2015 ), locates a change in
depth; exchanging internal states between checkpoints at selected
positions of the prompt, an application of activation patching
(Heimersheim & Nanda, 2024 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Vig et al., 2020 ), locates it in the prompt.

blocks.en:
Here we use authorship judgments as a test case for representation
versus readout under post-training. We studied six open-weight base
models and their post-trained versions with three corpora of German
texts: chat messages that students wrote for this study and that were
never published, so that they cannot have been part of any training
data; segments of articles from a local newspaper that, to our
knowledge, were not available in digital form and are therefore unlikely
to have been part of the training data; and summaries of textbook
chapters. First, we tested whether the information that distinguishes AI
from human texts is available in the models’ representations, and
compared it with simple text statistics. Second, we measured with signal
detection theory how the models’ own answers use this information, how
post-training changes it from stage to stage, whether labeled examples
can correct it, and whether a stated base rate moves the answers as it
would for an ideal observer. Third, we located the effect of
post-training by combining the lower and upper layers of base and
post-trained checkpoints (“model stitching”) and by exchanging
internal states between checkpoints at selected positions of the prompt
(“activation patching”). Fourth, because our corpora cannot be shared,
we repeated the central analyses with a judgment on public data that can
be reproduced in full, the truth of statements with and without
negation. Fifth, we manipulated the training data directly, in a
training study with control conditions, to test whether the training
signal sets the direction of the readout. We find that the authorship
information was readily available but that the models’ answers did not
use it, and that post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on
average. In the two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the weights that
carried this change resided in the early layers, and a sweep over layers
showed that from mid-depth onward the states at the positions after the
text, and not those of the text, transferred it between checkpoints;
below mid-depth, the text states contributed in one of the two models.
For negated statements, post-training acted in the opposite direction:
It repaired answers that several base models gave poorly although the
truth could be decoded at ceiling, through weights in the middle layers;
by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement,
and below that the representation of the statement itself contributed in
the four models in which we traced it, strongly in one of them. In the
training study, a small number of labeled examples shifted the readout
in the direction that their labels implied, with little change of the
probes at the text positions. A further judgment, whether a hotel review
is genuine, gave less conclusive results (Appendix C). Insofar as the
representation of the text is concerned, our results are largely
consistent with the superficial alignment hypothesis; at the same time,
they show that the change is not superficial in the sense of affecting
only the final stages of processing, and that it can make a judgment
considerably better or worse.

blocks.en: 2 Method
blocks.zh: 2 方法

blocks.en: 2.1 Materials
blocks.zh: 2.1 材料

blocks.en:
We used three corpora of German texts in which human-written texts are
matched with AI-generated counterparts. In each corpus, the human
original and all texts derived from it form one group ( source ),
and all analyses treat this group as the unit of resampling and
cross-validation, so that no result can rest on recognizing a topic.

与人工智能生成的对等器匹配。 每个人
原文和所有案文组成一个组(资料来源),
所有分析都把这一组人视为重新取样和
交叉验证,因此,任何结果都不得依赖于对某一专题的承认。

blocks.en:
Chat messages. The human messages were written in a session of an
experimental psychology lab course: Students were asked to write five
short chat or social-media posts each on current topics; example topics
were provided, but students were free to choose their own, and several
did so; not every student provided five messages. The messages were
never published. AI counterparts were generated by two large language
models (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4) on the same topics, in three steps.
All prompts placed the model in a private German group chat with friends
or family and asked for a single message of about one to four short
sentences, without hashtags. The basic prompt (“naive”) added only
that the message should sound natural, spontaneous, and everyday, as in
a real group chat rather than an essay. The style-matched prompt
additionally provided the other messages of the same student, on other
topics, as style references (tone, sentence length, directness,
colloquialism, punctuation, spontaneity). Finally, each style-matched
message was revised according to written feedback on what still sounded
AI-like, which the students gave on messages that they had not written
themselves (“optimized”). The students’ messages and their feedback
cannot be shared, because the students have not yet been asked for
consent to publication; the prompt templates, which contain placeholders
only, are included in the project repository ( prompts/ ).
Because AI and human messages differed considerably in length, we
truncated every message to its first 25 words and discarded shorter
messages. The resulting corpus comprised 300 texts (61 human, 239 AI)
from 61 groups. We verified the labels of this corpus: All human
messages are verbatim the students’ submissions, all AI messages trace
to the generation pipeline, and human participants of a separate
experiment recognized the messages in the labeled direction (AUC = .82;
Rosin & Laubrock, in preparation). Whether individual students used AI
tools to write their messages cannot be determined. Because the
generation pipeline had also stored the style-matched messages before
the feedback revision, we additionally scored these 122 messages (same
generators and truncation) as a control that separates the effect of
style matching from that of the revision.

blocks.en:
Newspaper segments. Articles written by a local journalist for a
local newspaper, which to our knowledge were not available in digital
form and are therefore unlikely to have been part of any model’s
training data, were paired with generated articles. For each article, a
locally run language model (Gemma 4 27B) extracted a summary of the
topic, the key facts (names, places, dates, numbers), and the length and
number of paragraphs, and it derived a profile of the author’s style
from the author’s other articles (leave-one-out). GPT-5.4 then wrote an
article of the same length and paragraph count that incorporated all key
facts, either from the topic and facts alone (“naive”) or additionally
following the style profile (“style-matched”); both prompts were
written in English, did not use web search, and instructed the model not
to reveal AI authorship. The style-matched articles were finally revised
to avoid nine surface features that the students of the lab course had
identified as AI markers in a sample of the articles (e.g., dashes,
lists of exactly three items, “not only … but also”
constructions, effusive closing sentences, uniform paragraph lengths,
too few numbers; “optimized”). The templates for the extraction and
writing steps are included in the project repository; the revision
prompt, which contains the students’ list of features, is not. We used
the 103 segments (38 human, 65 AI) from 14 articles that had been
presented in a human judgment experiment, each preceded by its headline
and subheadline, as in that experiment. These texts are confidential and
were processed only on university machines.

blocks.en: 2.2 Models
blocks.zh: 2.2 模式

blocks.en:
We studied six open-weight base models with 4 to 12 billion parameters
from four developers (Table 1): Gemma 3 (Gemma Team et al., 2025 ), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025 ), OLMo 2 (Team OLMo et al., 2025 ), OLMo 3 (Team Olmo et al., 2026 ), and Apertus
(Hernández-Cano et al., 2026 ;
Project Apertus et al., 2026 ).
For each base model, we compared the pretrained model with its final
post-trained version. We included the OLMo and Apertus models because
they are open beyond their weights: Their training data are known, and
for these three base models the developers released checkpoints after
each stage of post-training, which allowed us to follow the change step
by step: OLMo 2 7B (base, supervised fine-tuning [SFT], direct
preference optimization [DPO], and a final reinforcement-learning
stage with verifiable rewards), Apertus 1.5 8B (base, SFT, reinforcement
learning, DPO, and a final alignment stage), and OLMo 3 7B, for which
two lines of post-training start from the same base model (one optimized
for explicit reasoning, “Think”, one for conversation, “Instruct”)
and a third applies reinforcement learning to the base model without any
SFT (“RL-Zero”).

blocks.en:
2.3 Eliciting authorship
judgments
blocks.zh:
2.3 以利诱作者
判决

blocks.en:
We asked every model whether a text had been written by a human or
generated by an AI, in German, and read the answer off the model’s
next-word probabilities rather than from generated text. In the plain
completion format (“raw”), which works for base and post-trained
models alike, the prompt stated that the following text had been written
either by a human or by an AI, presented the text in quotation marks,
and asked: “Wurde dieser Text von einem Menschen geschrieben oder von
einer KI generiert? Antworte mit einem Wort (Mensch oder KI).” followed
by “Antwort:”. Post-trained models were in addition queried with their
own chat template (“chat”), with the system message “Du bewertest
Texte.” and the same question as user message. For reasoning models
whose template opens a reasoning block, the block was closed empty, so
that the next word is the answer.

blocks.en:
The decision variable was the difference in log probability between the
two answers, dv = log P(“KI”) − log P(“Mensch”). Each answer
probability summed over its spellings with and without a leading space
and included the probability that the word ends after the answer tokens
(Pimentel & Meister, 2024 ). To remove position
effects, every text was judged with both orders of the answer options
(“Mensch oder KI”, “KI oder Mensch”), and dv was averaged over the
two orders. As a manipulation check, we recorded the answer probability,
i.e., the summed probability of the two answers; conditions in which a
model placed less than 30% of its probability on the two answers were
excluded from inferential comparisons.

即两个答案的总概率;

blocks.en:
2.4 Signal detection measures and
statistics
blocks.zh:
2.4 信号探测措施和
统计

blocks.en:
Treating AI texts as signal, we computed sensitivity as d′ = √2 ·
z(AUC), where AUC is the area under the ROC curve of dv. For this
transformation, the AUC is limited to the interval [1/(2m), 1 −
1/(2m)], where m is the size of the smaller class, so that d′ has a
maximum that depends on the number of texts (e.g., 3.64 for 100
statement pairs and 4.54 for 748); values at this maximum mean that all
or nearly all pairs were ordered correctly (any AUC at or above the
bound yields the maximum), and differences near it are compressed. This
measure does not depend on where the model sets its decision threshold,
and negative values indicate that the model judges AI texts as less
AI-like than human texts. As a measure of response bias, we computed the
criterion c at the model’s natural threshold (dv = 0), with a log-linear
correction of hit and false-alarm rates (Hautus, 1995 ); positive values
indicate a bias toward answering “Mensch”. Because dv is a graded
preference, d′ characterizes how the evidence for the answer is ordered
across texts, in the manner of a confidence-rating ROC, even where the
binary answer hardly varies; c describes where the order-averaged dv
places the threshold and is not the criterion of any single prompt,
since the binary answers often depended on the order of the answer
options (Section 3.1). To test whether signal detection theory describes
the models’ judgments, we manipulated the response bias in two ways that
should leave the sensitivity unchanged: the order of the two answer
options, and a sentence stating the share of AI texts in the study (20,
50, or 80%), added to the plain prompt. For each single prompt
condition, we computed d′ and c from the dv of that prompt alone and
estimated the changes between conditions with a grouped bootstrap; where
a model gave the same answer to at least 98% of the texts, c is close
to its bound and can hardly move. To measure how strongly a model uses
the stated base rate, we computed for every text the shift of dv between
the prompts stating 20% and 80% AI texts and compared its mean with
the shift of the prior log-odds, ln(.8/.2) − ln(.2/.8) = ln 16 = 2.77
nats, by which an ideal observer would shift the posterior log-odds of
every text. The base-rate sentence named the share of AI texts first
(“In dieser Studie wurden etwa 20 % der Texte von einer KI generiert
und etwa 80 % von Menschen geschrieben.”); for Gemma 3 4B, OLMo 2 and
OLMo 3 Think, the manipulation was repeated with the human share named
first. Confidence intervals (95%) were obtained by a grouped bootstrap
that resampled whole source groups (1,000–2,000 resamples). The AUC,
and hence d′, as well as hit and false-alarm rates are computed within
each class and therefore do not depend on the unequal numbers of AI and
human texts (chats: 239 vs. 61; newspaper segments: 65 vs. 38); the
class proportions affect only the precision of the estimates, which is
limited by the smaller class and by the number of independent groups.
For the same reason, the probes were fitted with balanced class weights.

blocks.en:
To isolate the effect of post-training from the effect of the prompt
format, we compared each post-trained checkpoint with its base model on
the identical raw prompt (“clean” contrasts), computing the difference
in d′ on the same texts with a paired grouped bootstrap. Comparisons
across formats (base raw versus post-trained chat) are reported but
marked as confounded. p-values were obtained from a z-test with the
bootstrap standard error and corrected for multiple comparisons with the
Holm procedure within the family of the 18 comparisons between final and
base model on the identical prompt, which address our hypothesis; as a
stricter check, we report the Holm correction across all tested
contrasts, and the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure as a secondary
correction (Appendix G). The summary inference rests on the model family
as the unit (Section 3.2).

blocks.en: 2.5 Probes and baselines
blocks.zh: 2.5 探测器和基线

blocks.en:
To assess whether the authorship information is available in a model’s
internal representation, we trained linear probes on the activations of
the residual stream at the last position of the prompt, i.e., where the
answer is formed, for every layer. Each probe consisted of
standardization, a principal component rotation, and an L2-regularized
logistic regression whose regularization strength was selected by an
inner grouped cross-validation (standardization and rotation were fitted
on the whole training fold, so that the inner validation folds entered
these unsupervised steps; the held-out fold of the outer
cross-validation entered none; a strictly nested version, in which all
steps were refitted within each inner split, changed the probe d′ for
the short chats by −0.03 on average, with a range from −0.20 to +0.12
across the base and final checkpoints of the six families). Performance
was estimated out of fold with a 10-fold cross-validation that held out
whole source groups, and expressed as d′ (AUC). As a check, the same
procedure was repeated with labels shuffled within source groups. For
comparisons across models, we report the probe at a fixed relative depth
of two thirds of the network.

blocks.en:
To determine how much of this information is specific to the models, we
compared the probes with four baselines under the same cross-validation
scheme: logistic regressions on character n-grams (2–4) and on word
n-grams (1–2), both with TF-IDF weighting, on 14 surface statistics
(e.g., text length, word and sentence length, type-token ratio,
punctuation), and a probe on the average input embedding of the text
tokens (i.e., before any processing by the network). As an externally
trained reference, we applied EditLens (Thai et al., 2025 ), a detector based on
Llama 3.2 3B that was trained on English texts to estimate the extent of
AI editing; we re-implemented its published inference procedure and ran
it locally.

blocks.en: 2.6 In-context examples
blocks.zh: 2.6 文中的例子

blocks.en:
To test whether the models’ judgments reflect a belief that labeled
examples can correct, we placed k = 2, 8, or 16 labeled examples (half
human, half AI) before each text, in the same format as the target
question and with the correct answer filled in. Examples were drawn from
source groups other than that of the target text (for the chats, from
other authors) and truncated to 200 tokens. We used four fixed example
sets per condition; because few-shot answers are sensitive to the label
of the last example, the last label alternated between example sets.

人,半AI),在每条文字之前,与目标格式相同.

其他作者),并缩短为200个令牌. 我们用了四个固定的例子

blocks.en: 2.7 Causal interventions
blocks.zh: 2.7 因果关系干预

blocks.en:
We used three interventions, which are illustrated in Figure 2. All of
them change internal states or weights of the model during a
computation, which can be repeated at will with and without the
intervention.
blocks.zh:
我们使用了三种干预措施,如图2所示。 全体
a/ 改变模型的内部状态或重量
计算,可以任意重复,也可以不重复
干预。

blocks.en:
Steering. As a check on how the answer depends on the represented
information at the position where it is produced (Appendix D), we added
a vector to the residual stream at the last prompt position after a
given layer and measured the change in the answer score dv (Section
2.3). The authorship (or truth) direction was the difference between the
mean activations of the two classes, estimated for each text from other
source groups (7-fold cross-fitting). Steps were expressed in units of
the within-class standard deviation along this direction; the primary
test used ±2 SD, and we recorded a dose-response curve (±1, 2, 4, and 6
SD). The directional effect of a direction was half the difference
between the changes in dv for positive and negative steps. As null
controls, we used 50 random directions within the subspace spanned by
the 20 leading principal components of the within-class activations and
50 mean differences between random halves of the texts within each
class, each drawn once and applied to all texts. Controls took steps of
the same length as the authorship direction (norm-matched) or, in a
second run, of ±2 SD along their own direction (scale-matched). The
p-value of a direction was its rank among the absolute control effects
(two-sided; minimum 1/101). As a positive control, we used the direction
along which the model’s own answers vary (the decision direction). We
also report, per cell, the share of shifted texts whose projection
stayed within the 1st–99th percentile of the observed texts, and the
effect of a shift by one class-mean distance, extrapolated from the ±1
SD step. To make this number of directions feasible, the prompt up to
the last position was processed once per text and its cached activations
were reused for all steering settings, which reproduced the scores of
the uncached computation in a check on three statements with all
steering settings (102 scores: r = .999, largest difference 0.06 nats).
Steering was run for 25 cells (model × corpus × layer; Table D1 in
Appendix D).

blocks.en:
Model stitching. Model stitching combines parts of different
networks (Bansal et al., 2021 ; Lenc & Vedaldi, 2015 ). For the models with
stage-wise checkpoints, we combined the embedding and the first ℓ layers
of one checkpoint with the remaining layers, final normalization and
output layer of another, passing the residual stream at the junction on
unchanged. Stitching without an adapter is justified because both
checkpoints derive from the same pretrained weights; we verified this by
linear centered kernel alignment (CKA; Kornblith et al., 2019 ), a measure of how
similarly two sets of activations for the same inputs are arranged,
which is 1 for identical arrangements irrespective of a rotation of the
activation space, between the activations of base and post-trained
checkpoints, by the perplexity of each stitched model on 40 texts, and
by checking the two extremes: With ℓ = 0 (only the embedding from the
other checkpoint) and with ℓ = L (all layers from the other checkpoint,
but the own final normalization and output layer), d′ was within 0.05 of
the respective unstitched checkpoint in 15 of 16 cases (largest
difference 0.12). As a control task, we stitched the same checkpoints on
statements of diverse facts (counterfact), which base and SFT models
judged alike; for authorship, stitching and patching were run on the
textbook summaries and the short chats, and patching was repeated with a
prompt that placed the question before the text. We also exchanged only
the attention blocks or only the feed-forward blocks (each with its
normalization) of the first ℓ layers.
blocks.zh:
模型缝合。 模型缝合不同部分
网络(Bansal等人,2021年;Lenc & Vedaldi,2015年)。 对模型
阶段性的检查站,我们合并了嵌入层和第一层
一个检查站,其余各层,最后正常化和
另一个输出层,通过交叉点上的剩余流
不变。 没有适配器的跳槽是有道理的,因为

blocks.en:
Activation patching. Activation patching replaces internal states
of a model with those obtained under different conditions (Heimersheim
& Nanda, 2024 ; Meng et
al., 2023 ; Vig et al., 2020 ); here, the states came from
a different checkpoint (cf. Prakash et al., 2024 ). Stitching without
an adapter at layer ℓ is the special case in which the full residual
stream is exchanged at all positions. To separate the representation of
the text from the processing at the positions that follow it, we ran the
donor checkpoint over every prompt, stored its residual stream after
decoder layer k (i.e., the output of layer k, counted from 1) at all
prompt positions, and then ran the recipient checkpoint with its
residual stream after layer k replaced by the donor’s at a selected set
of positions: the tokens of the text (or statement), the positions
before the text (the instruction), the positions after the text
(question, instruction to answer with one word, and answer cue), the
tokens of the question line only, the final position only, or all
positions. The effect of an exchange is reported as the d′ of the
patched recipient or as the share of the difference in d′ between the
two unpatched checkpoints that the exchange transferred. A share above
100% or below 0% means that the hybrid lies outside the range of the
two checkpoints; where a checkpoint is at the maximum d′, shares are
compressed and a small disruption cannot be seen.

blocks.en:
To test whether the results generalize beyond authorship, we applied the
same analyses to two further judgments on publicly available data, for
which the correct answer is known as well.

blocks.en:
Truth judgments. We used three statement sets from Marks &
Tegmark ( 2024 ), each
consisting of 748 matched pairs of a true and a false statement that
differ in a single fact: simple geographic statements (“The city of
Bokaro is in India.”), the same statements negated (“The city of
Bokaro is not in China.”), and statements on diverse facts
(counterfact; one true and one false statement with the same subject and
relation, 748 pairs drawn with a fixed seed). The models were asked “Is
the following statement true or false?” and answered with “True” or
“False”; dv was the log-odds of the two answers, computed and averaged
over both answer orders as for authorship. In the chat format, the
system prompt was “You evaluate statements.” The pair formed the unit
of resampling and cross-validation.

Deceptive reviews. The Deceptive Opinion Spam Corpus (Ott et al., 2011 , 2013 ) contains 1,600 reviews of
20 hotels in Chicago, half of them written by guests (truthful) and half
by crowd workers who had never stayed at the hotel (deceptive), each in
a positive and a negative version. Human readers judge these reviews
close to chance, whereas classifiers on word frequencies separate them
well (Ott et al., 2011 ). The

guest about an actual stay; a deceptive review was written by someone
who has never stayed at the hotel.”), and the models answered with
“Truthful” or “Deceptive”; the system prompt in the chat format was
“You evaluate hotel reviews.” The hotel formed the unit of resampling
and cross-validation.

blocks.en:
For both judgments, we used the same six base models as for authorship,
with all post-training stages for OLMo 2, Apertus 1.5 and OLMo 3 Think,
and the base and final models for Gemma 3 4B, Gemma 3 12B and Qwen3 8B.
Probes were logistic regressions (L2 penalty, C = 0.01) on the
activations at the last prompt position at two thirds of the network
depth, evaluated out of fold. For the negated statements, we
additionally applied a probe trained on the simple geographic statements
of the same checkpoint (transfer probe), which tests whether one truth
direction also covers negated statements (Marks & Tegmark, 2024 ). Model stitching and
activation patching were carried out as for authorship, for both further
judgments, but only where there was a change to locate: in models whose
answers changed substantially with post-training and whose base models
placed at least 30% of their probability on the two answer words, the
criterion used for authorship (Table 2). For the negated statements,
these were OLMo 2 and Apertus (base vs. SFT, 300 pairs); the Gemma 3
base models fell below this criterion (18% and 25%), and the base
models of Qwen3 and OLMo 3 already judged the negated statements
perfectly. Because the two models differed in where the repair appeared
(Section 3.6), we later added the patching across layers for the two
Gemma 3 models as an exception to this criterion; their results are
reported with this caveat. For the reviews, these were Gemma 3 4B, which
lost sensitivity, and Qwen3 8B, which gained (base vs. final model; 800
pairs for stitching, 400 for patching); OLMo 2, Apertus and OLMo 3
changed little, and Gemma 3 12B, added later for consistency, was not
localized. For the statements on diverse facts, post-training changed
the answers too little in any model.

blocks.en:
Probe transfer between checkpoints. To test whether post-training
changes the geometry of the representation, we trained a probe at each
layer on the activations of one checkpoint and tested it on those of the
other (base vs. final model, both directions; grouped five-fold
cross-validation over the same items). Each checkpoint was standardized
with the statistics of its own training folds, so that the test concerns
the direction that separates the classes. The transfer deficit is the
loss in d′ relative to the probe trained and tested on the same
checkpoint, averaged over both directions. For the authorship corpora,
the analysis was carried out both for the last prompt position and for
the mean over the text positions.

blocks.en: 2.9 Training study
blocks.zh: 2.9 培训研究

blocks.en:
To test causally whether the training signal sets the direction of the
readout, we fine-tuned the OLMo 2 7B base model under five conditions
that differed only in a small set of added judgments. Every run
contained the same 20,000 conversations, sampled proportionally from all
parts of the model’s original supervised fine-tuning mixture (Tülu 3;
Lambert et al., 2025 ). The
conditions added 1,994 authorship judgments in the format of our
experiments (plain prompt, random answer order) with correct labels
(C1), with labels that followed a formality stereotype (C2), or with
random labels (C3), or no judgments at all (C0). A further condition
(C4) added the same texts with an unrelated judgment in the same layout
(whether the text is about politics, business, or society; answers
“Ja”/“Nein”; labels from the newspaper section), so that it
practiced a binary judgment of a text without the authorship question.
The judged texts were German news articles that are disjoint from our
test corpora: human articles from the online edition of the Austrian
daily DER STANDARD (10kGNAD; Block, 2019 ; derived from Schabus et
al., 2017 ), shortened to
25, 80, or 150 words, and AI articles that Qwen3 8B and Gemma 3 12B
(instruction-tuned versions) wrote on the same topics and sections,
shortened to the same lengths; each topic contributed either its human
or its AI text. For C2, the more formal half of each true class,
according to a score combining mean word length, the share of long
words, and the share of capitalized nouns, was labeled “KI”, so that
the labels were independent of the true authorship (50% agreement) and
followed the stereotype alone. Fine-tuning used low-rank adapters
[LoRA; Hu et al. ( 2021 ); rank 16,
all attention and feed-forward projections, learning rate
10 −4 , one epoch, three seeds per condition], with
the loss on the assistant turns of the conversations and on the answer
word of the judgments. We evaluated the final adapters on our three
authorship corpora and on 400 held-out news items (plain prompt, both
answer orders), and we analyzed their representations with probes and
probe transfer as in Section 2.8. The official SFT checkpoint of OLMo 2
served as a reference.

blocks.en:
To test whether the answers after training with valid news labels follow
what distinguishes AI from human news, we fitted a probe on the held-out
news in the base model (text positions, layers 20 and 24), applied it
unchanged to the short chats, and computed for every fine-tuned model
the Spearman correlation across the 300 chats between the probe score
and the answer score dv (pooled and within each class; means over the
three seeds; grouped bootstrap over source groups; differences between
conditions on the same resamples). The prediction was a positive
correlation for C1 that exceeds those of C0, C3, and C4. As a control
that uses no activations, we repeated the test with logistic regressions
on word n-grams (1–2) and character n-grams (2–4) of the same held-out
news, and computed partial rank correlations of each predictor with dv
controlling for the other. We also computed the cosine between the
direction that separates AI from human news at the last prompt position
of a fine-tuned model (difference of class means, or weight vector of a
probe) and the direction along which its answers to the chats vary
(difference between chats above and below the median dv, or ridge
regression of dv on the activations), with 1,000 random directions as a
reference; all variants are reported.

blocks.en: 2.10 Implementation
blocks.zh: 2.10 执行情况

blocks.en:
All models were run in bfloat16 precision with the Hugging Face transformers library (version 5.22.2; for Apertus, the
developers’ fork of version 5.18) and PyTorch 2.6, on NVIDIA A100 GPUs
(40 GB) of the university’s high-performance computing cluster and on a
local workstation. Gradients for the supplementary readout analysis were
computed with gradient checkpointing, which leaves them unchanged. All
analysis code is available in the project repository
(https://github.com/laubrock-lab/represented-but-misread).

blocks.en:
The newspaper texts are unpublished and confidential, the human chat
messages were written by students who have not yet been asked for
consent to publication, and the human textbook summaries are protected
by copyright. Therefore, these texts cannot be shared. The two further
judgments (Section 2.8) use publicly available data (Marks & Tegmark, 2024 ; Ott et al., 2011 , 2013 ). For the negated
statements, the repository contains one entry point that reruns the
analyses from the public statement sets and a check against the values
reported here; for the reviews, it contains the code but no such entry
point. The human texts of the training study (Section 2.9) are public
(Block, 2019 ); the AI texts that
we generated for it are not yet released. All code and the tables of
derived results from which the reported numbers are taken are available
in the project repository. The per-text model outputs for the authorship
corpora are not included, because their identifiers refer to unpublished
texts.

blocks.en: 3 Results
blocks.zh: 3 结果

blocks.en:
We first report the authorship judgments, for which we used our own
corpora: whether the information is available and whether the answers
use it (Section 3.1), how post-training changed the answers (Section
3.2), how the models used a stated base rate (Section 3.3), and where in
the network the change acts (Sections 3.4 and 3.5). Because these
corpora cannot be shared, Section 3.6 reports a judgment on public data
that can be reproduced in full, the truth of negated statements, for
which post-training changed the answers in the opposite direction.
Section 3.7 reports a training study that tests what sets the direction
of the change. A further judgment, whether a hotel review is genuine,
gave less conclusive results and is reported in Appendix C. Unless
stated otherwise, sensitivity is expressed as d′ estimated from the area
under the ROC curve, with 95% confidence intervals from a grouped
bootstrap.

blocks.en:
We used three corpora of German texts that each pair human-written texts
with AI-generated counterparts: short chat messages truncated to 25
words (300 texts from 61 human originals), segments of local newspaper
articles (103 segments from 14 articles), and textbook summaries (238
texts, 119 matched human–AI pairs; Rosin & Laubrock, in preparation).
In all analyses, texts derived from the same human original form one
group, so that a model, a probe, or a bootstrap resample never profits
from recognizing a topic. Positive values of d′ indicate that AI texts
are judged as more AI-like than human texts, negative values indicate
the reverse.

blocks.en:
Is the information that separates AI from human texts available to the
models at all? We first answered this question with linear probes, i.e.,
simple classifiers that are trained on a model’s internal activations to
predict authorship and are evaluated on held-out texts. At a fixed depth
of two thirds of the network, probes separated AI from human texts well
in every model and corpus, with a median d′ of 1.35 for the short chats
(range across model conditions 0.95–1.80), 2.66 for the newspaper
segments (1.65–3.14), and 3.70 for the textbook summaries (2.36–3.73).
When the authorship labels were shuffled within groups, probe
performance dropped to chance (mean AUC = .50), which rules out that the
probes merely memorized the training texts.

However, this information is not specific to the internal machinery of
language models. Classifiers trained on simple word frequencies reached
the same or higher sensitivity than the probes (short chats: d′ = 1.73
[1.44, 2.06]; newspaper segments and textbook summaries: AUC ≥
.99 1 1 1 When nearly all pairs of texts are ordered correctly, the
AUC-based d′ approaches a maximum that depends on the number of texts
(d′ = 3.73 for the textbook summaries and 3.14 for the newspaper
segments); for such near-perfect classifiers, we therefore report the
AUC. ), and a probe on the average input embedding of the text, i.e.,
before any processing by the network, performed about as well as probes
on deep layers (short chats: d′ = 1.48). Holding out whole authors
instead of single originals did not change this picture (word
frequencies: d′ = 1.79). A detector that was trained by others to
recognize AI-edited English text (EditLens; Thai et al., 2025 ) transferred to our
German material in a graded manner, reaching an AUC of .99 for the
textbook summaries, .73 for the newspaper segments, and .57 for the
short chats (Figure 3). Thus, the cues that distinguish AI from human
texts are present and readily accessible, both in the texts themselves
and in the models’ representations; they consist largely of ordinary
lexical and stylistic regularities. In terms of Brunswik’s lens model,
the environment offers valid cues.

blocks.en:
These cues, however, are specific to the corpus. When a probe trained on
the newspaper segments was applied unchanged to the short chats, it
separated them with the wrong sign (Gemma 3 4B and 12B, six model
conditions: median d′ = −0.46 at the last prompt position and −0.48 for
the averaged text positions; Qwen3: −0.48 and −0.60), and the authorship
direction of the news pointed slightly against that of the chats (cosine
about −0.2). In the opposite direction, probes trained on the chats
transferred weakly but with the correct sign (median d′ = 0.37–0.87).
Hence, there is no single authorship direction that holds across text
types: Properties that mark AI texts in one corpus can mark human texts
in another. This is important for reading the answers below, because a
judge that applies one fixed policy to all texts can be above chance on
one corpus and below chance on another.

blocks.en:
When the models were asked directly whether a text had been written by a
human or by an AI, their answers did not reflect this information. Table
2 summarizes the order-averaged sensitivity of the answers for the
pretrained base models and for the final post-trained models. Many cells
are close to chance, and a considerable number are clearly below it:
Qwen3-8B after post-training judged the newspaper segments with d′ =
−1.01 (raw prompt) and −1.30 (chat prompt), and Gemma 3 12B judged the
short chats with d′ = −0.81 and −1.09. Several models thus ordered the
texts inversely: What distinguished AI from human texts moved their
answers toward the wrong class. Note that these values were computed
from the graded preference of the model, i.e., the log-odds of “AI”
versus “human” for each text, which plays the role of a confidence
rating in a rating-scale ROC analysis. The binary answer itself often
did not vary: In 23 of the 36 conditions with the plain prompt (Table 2,
base and final models), the model gave the same answer to more than 95%
of the texts, and in several base models the share of “AI” answers
depended strongly on the order in which the two options were named
(e.g., OLMo 2 on the short chats: 89% vs. 0%). A negative d′ therefore
does not mean that the models gave many wrong binary answers. It means
that the graded evidence on which the answer is based was ordered the
wrong way round: human texts received a stronger preference for “AI”
than AI texts did. Such an inverse ordering cannot result from a
response bias, which only shifts the preference for all texts alike;
properties typical of human texts pushed the answer toward “AI”, and
properties typical of AI texts toward “human”.

blocks.en:
3.2 Post-training lowers the sensitivity of authorship
judgments
blocks.zh:
3.2 国家 培训后降低作者的敏感性
判决

blocks.en:
Base models were not uniformly better, but several of them discriminated
clearly above chance where their post-trained counterparts did not
(e.g., Gemma 3 12B on the textbook summaries, d′ = +1.64; OLMo 3 on the
newspaper segments, +0.60; Qwen3 on the textbook summaries, +0.55). To
test the effect of post-training without confounding it with the prompt
format, we compared each final model with its base model on the
identical plain prompt. Of these 18 comparisons, 14 showed a decrease.
Because each model family contributes three corpora and each corpus six
families, the 18 comparisons are not independent. Our primary test
therefore treats the model family as the unit: A t-test over the six
family means yielded a mean change of Δd′ = −0.34 [−0.56, −0.11]
(t(5) = −3.82, p = .012); all six families showed a decrease on average,
two of them only slightly (OLMo 2: −0.10; OLMo 3 Think: −0.06). A
multilevel random-effects model with random effects for model family,
corpus, and cell gave the same estimate (−0.33 [−0.53, −0.13]); its
nominal test (t(17) = −3.54, p = .003) uses residual degrees of freedom
and is likely too liberal with six families. Heterogeneity between cells
was considerable (I² = 83%). Restricted to the nine comparisons in
which both models placed at least half of their probability on the two
answer words, the estimate was similar but less precise (−0.31 [−0.64,
0.01], p = .057; four families). In the three comparisons in which the
binary answers varied in both the base and the final model (Gemma 3 12B
on the short chats and the textbook summaries, Gemma 3 4B on the short
chats), post-training lowered d′ in all three cases (−0.45 to −0.95).
Per corpus, with six families each, the decrease was reliable for the
newspaper segments (−0.42 [−0.75, −0.08], p = .024), but not for the
textbook summaries (−0.41 [−0.85, 0.04], p = .066) or the short
chats (−0.19 [−0.55, 0.16], p = .22).

blocks.en:
Did the decline depend on the wording of the prompt? We repeated all
comparisons with a paraphrased instruction and question and with the
question placed before the text. Across the three prompts, the mean
change over the six family means (each the mean of nine comparisons) was
Δd′ = −0.29 [−0.54, −0.03] (t(5) = −2.88, p = .035), with a decrease
in five of six families and in 39 of the 54 comparisons. A multilevel
model with additional random effects for the prompt gave the same
estimate (−0.29), with variance components near zero for prompt and
corpus, but it is not informative as a test, because the prompt and the

blocks.en:
For OLMo 2, Apertus 1.5, and OLMo 3, the developers released checkpoints
after each stage of post-training, which allowed us to ask when the
change occurs. On the textbook summaries, it occurred in OLMo 2 and
Apertus at the first, supervised stage (supervised fine-tuning, SFT), in
which the model learns to imitate example answers. For OLMo 2 on the
textbook summaries, d′ fell from −0.12 (base) to −0.50 after SFT and
then remained stable (−0.46 after preference optimization, −0.44 after
the final reinforcement-learning stage). For Apertus, d′ fell from +0.43
to −0.04 after SFT and stayed near zero through the subsequent stages
(0.00, −0.03, −0.04). The other corpora and the OLMo 3 lines, for which
stage-wise checkpoints exist as well, mostly gave the same picture: On
the newspaper segments, d′ fell at the supervised stage in OLMo 2 (−0.14
to −0.54), OLMo 3 Think (+0.60 to +0.08), and OLMo 3 Instruct (+0.60 to
−0.28), and on the short chats in Apertus (−0.23 to −0.73). There were
two exceptions: OLMo 3 Instruct on the short chats declined only at the
preference stage (−0.09 after SFT, −0.30 after DPO), and Apertus on the
newspaper segments did not change clearly at any stage (+0.07 to −0.07).
In most cases, the later, preference-based stages thus added little to a
change that was already complete after imitation learning.

blocks.en:
Could the post-trained models simply hold a wrong belief about what AI
texts look like, a belief that a few correctly labeled examples would
correct? We tested this by placing 2, 8, or 16 labeled examples from
other sources before each text (four different sets of examples; d′
computed per set and averaged; Figure 4B). With 16 examples, d′ rose
reliably in 8 of 11 model conditions on the short chats and in 4 of 6 on
the textbook summaries, whereas two examples hardly helped. The gains of
base and post-trained models did not differ consistently: The difference
was reliable in two of five comparisons, with opposite signs (OLMo 2 on
the chats, where the base model gained more, +0.54 [0.27, 0.83];
Qwen3 on the textbook summaries, where the post-trained model gained
more, −0.31 [−0.55, −0.09]; Table E1). The gap between them
persisted: After 16 examples, the post-trained model was still less
sensitive than its base model in all five comparisons (e.g., Gemma 3 4B
on the short chats: +0.48 vs. −0.27; Qwen3: +0.15 vs. −0.17), and the
post-trained models of Gemma 3 4B and Qwen3 remained below chance on the
chats (Appendix E). Labeled examples do not give a model a new ability;
they only show which properties go with which label in the material at
hand. That they raised d′ in base and post-trained models alike
therefore indicates that part of the failure lies in which properties
the models take as signs of AI authorship, i.e., in a mapping that
information can correct, and not in an inability to tell the texts
apart. Because the examples did not remove the difference between base
and post-trained models, however, such a correctable mapping does not
account for the deficit that post-training introduced.

blocks.en:
Which properties of the texts did the answers follow? A lens-model
analysis of the short chats (Appendix B) showed that the answers of most
post-trained models weighted 34 text properties in the direction
opposite to their validity (cross-validated matching index G: Gemma 3 4B
−.49, Gemma 3 12B −.58, Qwen3 −.61, Apertus after SFT −.57). They took
long words, adjectives, nouns, and low readability as signs of AI
authorship, whereas the AI messages in this corpus were more verbal and
lexically more diverse than the human ones. In Qwen3, this weighting was
already present in the base model (−.53); OLMo 2, whose answers on the
chats improved slightly, weighted the properties in the opposite way
after SFT (+.37). The properties that the students had named as typical
of AI text (e.g., dashes, perfect capitalization) were barely valid in
the truncated messages and barely used by the models, and style-matched
messages that had not been revised according to the students’ feedback
were judged like the revised ones (change in AUC between −.03 and +.04
for every model).

blocks.en:
3.3 Criterion, sensitivity, and the use of a stated base
rate

3.3 标准、敏感性和使用说明的基地

blocks.en:
Is signal detection theory an appropriate description of these
judgments? Its central assumption is that manipulations of the response
bias move the criterion but leave the sensitivity unchanged. This held
approximately. Raising the stated share of AI texts from 20% to 80%
moved the criterion in 48 of 72 comparisons (model × checkpoint × corpus
× answer order), in all of them toward “AI” and reliably so in 42
(mean |Δc| across all comparisons = 1.19); in the
remaining 24 comparisons, c did not change, because the model gave the
same answer to nearly every text at either share. The sensitivity was
not strictly invariant, however: d′ changed by 0.14 on average, without
a consistent direction, and the bootstrap interval of the change
excluded zero in 28 of the 72 comparisons. In the 14 comparisons in
which no condition was saturated, the criterion shifted reliably in all
14 and d′ in 3 (mean |Δd′| = 0.10). The order of the
answer options and the mere presence of the base-rate sentence also
acted mainly on the criterion (mean |Δc| = 0.78 and
0.42), and changed d′ by similar amounts (0.16 and 0.13, again without a
consistent direction; Appendix F). Thus, manipulations of the response
bias acted mainly on the criterion where the criterion could move, and
the criterion is a property of the model together with the prompt rather
than of the model alone. Because the accompanying changes of d′ were not
negligible relative to the effects reported below, we average d′ over
both answer orders and compare checkpoints only on identical prompts.

blocks.en:
How strongly did the models use the stated base rate? Any observer who
takes the stated share into account should answer “AI” more readily
when it is higher. A reference point for the size of this effect is an
ideal observer in a stationary environment, for whom the stated share is
the prior and changes nothing else: The log-odds of the answer then
shift by the same amount for every text, ln 16 = 2.77 nats between 20%
and 80%. We use this value as a reference, not as a norm that a
sensible judge must meet (in a changing environment, for instance,
weighting a stated base rate less can be adequate), and it applies to dv
only insofar as dv is read as the model’s posterior log-odds. The base
models shifted far less (mean shift of dv per model between 0.18 and
1.40 nats, i.e., 6–51% of the benchmark), and the shift was nearly
uniform across texts (between-text SD within a condition 0.08–0.33).
After post-training, five of the six models shifted more than the
benchmark (3.67–10.93 nats, i.e., 1.3–3.9 times the benchmark), and
the shift differed considerably between texts (SD up to 3.14); OLMo 3
Think was the exception (1.21 nats, as in its base model, 1.17). These
values were obtained with a base-rate sentence that named the share of
AI texts first. For the three families that fit the available GPUs, we
repeated the manipulation with the human share named first. The pattern
was the same, but the size of the shift depended on the wording in the
post-trained models: The base models again shifted too little (Gemma 3
4B: 0.16; OLMo 2: 1.35; OLMo 3: 1.07 nats), the post-trained models of
Gemma 3 4B and OLMo 2 again shifted more than the benchmark, but less
than with the first wording (5.61 vs. 10.65 and 4.37 vs. 5.39 nats), and
OLMo 3 Think again stayed below it (1.48). Post-training thus changed
the use of a stated base rate from underweighting to overweighting in
five of six model families, by a factor that depended on the model and
on the wording (Table F2); the second wording was not run for Apertus,
Qwen3, and Gemma 3 12B.

blocks.en:
Note that a shift in nats also depends on the overall scale of a model’s
log-odds, and this scale differed between checkpoints: Across texts of
the same class, dv varied far more in the post-trained models
(within-class SD per model 0.61–2.89 nats) than in the base models
(0.21–0.53). Relative to this spread, i.e., to the differences that the
models make between texts, the stated base rate already moved the base
models considerably (by 0.9–3.3 SD per model) and the post-trained
models somewhat more (2.0–5.3 SD); the relative shift increased with
post-training in five families and decreased in OLMo 3 Think (3.3 to 2.0
SD), and with the second wording it increased only in Gemma 3 4B (0.8 to
4.2 SD), not in OLMo 2 (2.5 to 2.4 SD). Thus, the post-trained models
gave more extreme log-odds in general, to the base rate as well as to
the texts; that the base rate gained weight relative to the texts holds
for most, but not all, models and wordings.

blocks.en:
3.4 Where the change acts: model stitching and activation
patching
blocks.zh:
3.4 国家 变化的作用:模型缝合和激活
补丁

blocks.en: Model stitching
blocks.zh: 模型缝合

blocks.en:
Where in the network does post-training make the difference? Because the
base and the post-trained checkpoints of a model share the same
architecture and start from the same weights, we could combine them: the
lower layers from one checkpoint and the upper layers from the other,
passing the internal state at the junction on unchanged (“model
stitching”). This test requires no probe and no statistic derived from
the answers; it only measures how well the combined model discriminates.
Two observations justified the procedure. First, the representations of
the texts themselves were highly similar in the base and the
post-trained checkpoints of the three models with stage-wise checkpoints
(linear CKA across layers 0.97–0.999 for OLMo 2, Apertus and OLMo 3;
textbook summaries), whereas the representations at the position where
the answer is formed differed considerably (0.44–0.99, median
0.65–0.85). Note that linear CKA without bias correction, computed here
on 238 texts in about 4,000 dimensions, is biased upward, so that values
near 1 are weak evidence of identity; the contrast between the text
positions and the answer position is the more informative result. Note
also that this was less so for the other families: In Gemma 3, even the
text representations changed noticeably, most at mid-depth (0.42–0.99,
median 0.80–0.83), and the answer position differed strongly (median
0.20–0.31), so that for Gemma 3 the claim that the text positions
changed little rests on the probe transfer alone (Section 3.5). Second,
every stitched model produced fluent text (perplexity 6.0–6.7 for
Apertus, 8.2–9.4 for OLMo 2), and, as a check of the implementation,
stitching at the very bottom or the very top reproduced the respective
parent model.

blocks.en:
If post-training changed only the final readout stage, the upper layers
should decide the outcome. This was not the case (Figure 5A). When the
first 8 of 32 layers of Apertus came from the base model and all layers
above from the SFT model, the combined model discriminated at least as
well as the base model (d′ = +0.59 [0.41, 0.80]; base +0.43).
Conversely, the first 8 layers of the SFT model sufficed to abolish the
base model’s discrimination, although all 24 layers above came from the
base model (−0.50 [−0.74, −0.25]). For OLMo 2, the first 16 base
layers restored base-level performance under SFT upper layers (−0.01
[−0.15, 0.14]; base −0.12, SFT −0.50), and the first 6 SFT layers
were sufficient to produce the full deficit (−0.48). Finer steps showed
that the change builds up gradually over several early layers rather
than in a single one (Apertus: layers 3–8; OLMo 2: layers 1–14).

blocks.en:
Note, however, that the hybrids did not always lie between their
parents. In Apertus, the first 8 SFT layers under base upper layers
judged worse than the SFT model itself (−0.50 vs. −0.04), with a reduced
probability on the two answer words (.39 vs. .68 for the base and .83
for the SFT model), and the first SFT layer alone under base upper
layers judged better than either parent (+0.73). Were these effects
artifacts of stitching as such? As a control, we stitched the same
checkpoints on a judgment that post-training had changed little, the
truth of statements on diverse facts (counterfact; Apertus: d′ = 1.37
base vs. 1.60 SFT; OLMo 2: 1.78 vs. 1.74, on the 300 pairs used for
stitching). There, all hybrids stayed within or close to the range of
their parents (largest deviation from the unstitched parents 0.02 for
Apertus and 0.08 for OLMo 2; none of 14 Apertus hybrids and one of 14
OLMo 2 hybrids reliably outside), whereas on the textbook summaries 6 of
18 Apertus hybrids and 4 of 18 OLMo 2 hybrids lay reliably outside
(largest deviation 0.46 and 0.15). Stitching thus does not disturb the
models’ judgments in general. The control does not show, however, that
the overshoot is specific to the judgment that post-training changed:
The control judgment was far from chance, with high answer probability,
whereas the textbook judgments were close to chance, where small
perturbations can reorder the texts. A judgment near chance that
post-training left unchanged would be the appropriate control, which we
did not run. The stitching results show that the early-layer weights of
a checkpoint suffice to carry the difference into an otherwise foreign
network; they do not by themselves show that the difference is computed
there.

On the short chats, on which post-training lowered the sensitivity of
Apertus (−0.23 to −0.73) and raised that of OLMo 2 (−0.07 to +0.38), the
early locus replicated in one direction only. The first 8 base layers of
Apertus restored the base level under SFT upper layers (−0.27), and the
first 4 base layers of OLMo 2 removed most of its gain (+0.10). The
first 8 SFT layers under base upper layers, however, did not produce the
effect of SFT in either model (Apertus: −0.31; OLMo 2: −0.07); it
appeared only with 16 SFT layers (−0.70 and +0.27). On the chats, the
early base layers were thus sufficient to remove the effect of SFT, but
the early SFT layers were not sufficient to produce it, in contrast to
the textbook summaries. No hybrid lay outside the range of its parents
on the chats. Note also that the effect to be localized is small for
OLMo 2 on this corpus.

blocks.en:
The stitching results implicate the early layers, but do not yet say
where in the prompt the change acts. In a language model, information
about the text reaches the answer through the positions that follow it:
the question “Was this text written by a human or generated by an
AI?”, the answer cue, and the last position, from which the answer is
produced and which itself reads the text at every layer. We therefore
exchanged the internal states between base and SFT checkpoints
selectively at different positions of the prompt (“activation
patching”): at the tokens of the text, at the instruction before the
text, at the question after the text, or at the final position only.

blocks.en:
At layer 16, the pattern was unambiguous and identical for both models
(Figure 5B, which shows the positions exchanged at this layer).
Exchanging the states of the text tokens changed nothing: Apertus after
SFT remained at chance when it received the base model’s text
representation (−0.11; SFT alone −0.04), and the base model kept its
sensitivity when it received the SFT model’s text representation (+0.43;
base alone +0.43). Exchanging only the states of the question positions
transferred the full difference in both directions: the base model’s
question states restored discrimination in the SFT model (Apertus:
+0.41; OLMo 2: +0.04, from −0.50), and the SFT model’s question states
abolished it in the base model (Apertus: −0.42; OLMo 2: −0.61, from
−0.12). The final position alone carried part of this effect in Apertus
(−0.08 and −0.15) and in OLMo 2 most of it in one direction (−0.06 from
−0.50) and about half in the other (−0.34 from −0.12). The same held for
the short chats, on which exchanging the text states changed nothing
(all changes ≤ 0.04), whereas the states after the text transferred the
difference: The SFT states made the base models judge like the SFT
models (Apertus: −0.23 → −0.75, SFT −0.73; OLMo 2: −0.07 → +0.34, SFT
+0.38), and the base states restored the base level in Apertus (−0.73 →
−0.27) and partly in OLMo 2 (+0.38 → +0.20). Within the positions after
the text, the tokens of the question itself carried little and the
answer cue most of the difference (e.g., Apertus base with SFT states at
the question tokens: −0.46; at all positions after the text: −0.75); the
final position alone carried between a third and two thirds. Because
post-training improved the judgments of OLMo 2 on the chats, the change
resided at the positions after the text regardless of its direction. At
layer 8, the picture was mixed (Figure S1, which adds this layer): in
Apertus, the text positions still had a partial effect, and in OLMo 2
even exchanging all positions transferred only part of the difference,
consistent with the stitching result that in OLMo 2 the change
accumulates up to about layer 14. Thus, at the middle of the network,
exchanging the states at the positions after the text (question and
answer cue) transferred the difference, and exchanging the text states
did not.

Activation patching across
layers
