blocks.en:
Patching at two layers can miss a contribution that is confined to other
layers, as the negated statements show (Section 3.6). We therefore
repeated the patching on the textbook summaries at 12 layers between 2
and 32 (Figure 6). In OLMo 2, the text states did not transfer the
difference at any layer, in either direction: The base model with the
SFT model’s text states stayed between −0.17 and −0.05 (unpatched
−0.12), and the SFT model with the base model’s text states between
−0.61 and −0.44 (unpatched −0.50). The states after the text transferred
the difference from layer 12 onward (base model with SFT states: −0.50
at layer 12 and −0.59 at layer 14; SFT model with base states: −0.02 at
layer 14). Below layer 12, the difference was distributed: Exchanging
all positions had the clearest effect (e.g., −0.48 for the base model at
layer 6), and the positions of the instruction before the text
transferred a reliable part by themselves (34–48% at layers 6 to 10
for the base model with SFT states; 32–51% at layers 8 to 12 in the
other direction), about as much as the positions after the text at these
layers. In Apertus, in contrast, the text states carried part of the
difference in the lower half of the network: With the SFT model’s text
states, the base model fell from 0.43 to 0.21–0.33 at layers 2 to 12
(22–46% of the difference between the checkpoints), and with the base
model’s text states, the SFT model rose from −0.04 to 0.10–0.26 at
layers 4 to 12 (30–64%); the bootstrap interval of the transferred
share excluded zero at layers 6 to 12 in the first direction and at
layers 4, 8, 10, and 12 in the second. From layer 14 onward, the text
states had no effect in either direction. The instruction positions
again carried a part in the lower layers (41–47% at layers 4 to 8 for
the SFT model with base states; inconsistent in sign in the other
direction). The SFT model’s states after the text lowered the base model
from layer 4 onward, by more than the whole difference between the
checkpoints (e.g., to −0.48 at layer 12, compared with −0.04 for the SFT
model), which again shows that hybrids produce effects of their own; in
the other direction, the base model’s states after the text restored the
SFT model partly at layers 6 to 12 (0.09–0.31), fully at layers 14 to
20 (0.41–0.61), and again only partly above (0.24–0.31 at layers 24 to
32, where exchanging all positions gave hardly more, 0.24–0.37; the
final normalization and output layer of the two checkpoints differ).
Note that the instruction before the text already names the two
alternatives (human or AI), so that the text is read with the judgment
in view, although before the question; a contribution of the text or
instruction states can therefore be specific to the judgment, and our
data do not decide whether the Apertus text-state effect is specific to
it or reflects a general change in how the lower layers encode text.
Thus, from layer 14 onward the difference between the checkpoints was
carried by the positions after the text in both models; below, the text
states contributed in Apertus but not in OLMo 2, and the instruction
positions contributed in both.

blocks.en:
In our default prompt, the question follows the text (the instruction
before the text names the two alternatives, but does not pose the
question). We also repeated the patching at layer 16 with the question
placed before the text, so that the text was read with the question
known. The decline persisted with this prompt (Apertus: +0.36 base
vs. −0.19 SFT; OLMo 2: +0.09 vs. −0.42). Table H1 (Appendix H) shows the
change of d′ for each set of positions (layer 16 only). Exchanging the
text states changed d′ by at most 0.12 (3–22% of the difference
between the checkpoints). The few positions after the text
(“Antwort:”) transferred the whole difference in one of the four cases
(Apertus SFT with base states: −0.19 → +0.44, more than the difference
itself) and 42–49% in the other three; the question before the text
transferred 18–53% in three cases and moved the Apertus base model
away from the SFT model (+0.36 → +0.55). The effects of the single sets
did not add up to the effect of exchanging all positions, so that the
states before, within, and after the text contributed jointly. Note also
that a missing effect of the text states at layer 16 does not show that
they are irrelevant, because the later positions have by then read the
recipient’s own text states in the layers below; with the default prompt
at layer 8, the text states did have an effect in Apertus. We therefore
conclude only that, at mid-depth, the difference between the checkpoints
was not carried by the text states alone, also when the text is read
with the question known. In summary, exchanging the text states at
mid-depth transferred little of the change, whereas exchanging the
states at the positions that follow the text transferred much or all of
it with the default prompt; in this sense, post-training changed how the
question takes up the text.

3.5 Probes across
checkpoints

3.5 跨度探测器
检查站

blocks.en:
If post-training leaves the representation intact and changes how it is
read out, a probe trained on the base model should work on the
post-trained model at the text positions, but less so at the position
where the answer is formed. This was the case wherever we could test it
(Figure S2), with qualifications. The comparison of the two sites exists
only for the authorship corpora (all six families); for the other
judgments, the activations were stored at the last position only, for
OLMo 2 and Apertus (all three sets) and for Gemma 3 4B and Qwen3
(reviews). At the text positions of the authorship corpora, probes
transferred between the base and the final checkpoints with little loss:
Averaged across models, the transfer deficit stayed at or below 0.15 d′
at every depth, and 94% of the single model × layer values were at or
below 0.10 (largest value 0.54, for OLMo 2 on the textbook summaries in
the top layers). Because the probes at the text positions were at their
maximum in 89% of these values for the textbook summaries and in 67%
for the newspaper segments, the test can only fail where they are not,
i.e., mainly for the short chats (within-checkpoint d′ = 1.30–2.48);
there, the largest deficit of any model was 0.16. At the last prompt
position, the deficit grew with depth, reaching on average 0.7 to 1.9 d′
in the upper third of the network for the authorship corpora and 0.5 to
1.1 d′ for the other judgments (with one exception: for OLMo 2 on the
negated statements, the upper layers showed no deficit). Probes still
transferred partially at this position (mean d′ in the upper third up to
2.0, averaged over both directions of transfer, but near zero for Gemma
3 4B on the newspaper segments), so the readout position was reorganized
rather than replaced. Probes that were trained and tested on the same
model version (base or post-trained) continued to decode the information
at the last position, but in four of the six families less well after
post-training on at least one corpus (upper third of the network, final
vs. base model: Gemma 3 4B, −0.52 on the newspaper segments and −0.90 on
the textbook summaries; Gemma 3 12B, −0.57 and −0.47; OLMo 3 Think,
−0.41 and −0.70; Qwen3, −0.38 on the textbook summaries). In Apertus,
the change was mixed (chats −0.26, newspaper segments +0.43), and in
OLMo 2 there was no decline. Post-training thus left the text positions
essentially unchanged where the test is informative, and both
reorganized and, in some models, degraded the information available at
the answer position.

The authorship corpora cannot be shared. Is the dissociation between
representation and answer, and its modification by post-training,
specific to them? We repeated the central analyses with truth judgments
on public statement sets (Section 2.8), whose main analyses (answers,
probes, stitching, and patching at two layers) can be rerun with one
script. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: It repaired
answers that the base models gave poorly. Table 3 summarizes the
results.

blocks.en:
Table 3 lists, for all six model families, the base model and the final
post-trained (instruction-tuned) model, and for the three families with
stage-wise checkpoints also the model after supervised fine-tuning. The
simple geographic statements, which we ran for OLMo 2 and Apertus only,
were judged at or near ceiling by all their checkpoints (d′ ≥ 4.38), so
that this set served only as a check. For the negated statements,
however, two base models showed a clear dissociation between
representation and answer: Probes decoded the truth of every statement
(AUC = 1), but the answers of the OLMo 2 base model used this
information only weakly (d′ = 0.80), and those of the Apertus base model
ordered the statements inversely (d′ = −0.88). Both base models answered
“False” almost always (criterion c = 2.6 and 3.0). Supervised
fine-tuning repaired the answers of both models, whereas the probes
remained at ceiling, and the final post-trained models kept this level.
The Gemma 3 models showed the same pattern between their base and final
versions, although their base models rarely answered with the two answer
words. The base models of Qwen3 and OLMo 3, in contrast, already judged
the negated statements perfectly; post-training left this unchanged in
Qwen3 and lowered it slightly in OLMo 3. Thus, post-training repaired
the readout of negation where the base model read it wrongly, but did
not improve it further where the base model read it correctly. A probe
trained on the simple statements of the same checkpoint suggests what
the base models’ answers followed: Applied to the negated statements, it
separated them with the wrong sign (OLMo 2: d′ = −1.28; Apertus: −1.43),
i.e., the general truth direction of the base models encoded whether
city and country belong together and ignored the negation; whether the
answers followed this direction item by item was not tested. After SFT,
the same probe separated the negated statements in the correct direction
(+0.69; +3.05). For the statements on diverse facts, post-training
changed the answers only slightly, except in OLMo 3, where answers and
probes declined together (answers 1.61 → 1.34; probes 1.89 → 1.64).

blocks.en:
Why did post-training change the answers for the negated statements but
hardly for the statements on diverse facts? The two sets differ in what
limits the answers. The statements on diverse facts are affirmative, and
judging them requires only that the fact is known: The probes were far
from their maximum, and the answers of the base models were already
close to the probes (e.g., OLMo 2: d′ = 1.79 for the answers vs. 2.15
for the probe), so that there was little represented information that
the answers failed to use. The negated statements require that the fact
is combined with the negation. The probes show that this combination is
available at the last prompt position of every model, but the answers of
several base models did not reflect it. Post-training thus changed the
answers where they fell short of what was represented, not where they
were limited by what the model knows.

blocks.en:
Where does the repair arise? We combined the lower layers of one
checkpoint with the upper layers of the other (model stitching; Section
2.7, Figure 2C; results in Figure 7A). Stitching located the repair in
the middle of the network rather than in the early layers. In OLMo 2,
the first 8 base layers combined with all upper SFT layers still judged
at the level of the SFT model (d′ = 3.76 [3.47, 4.15], i.e., above
it, another case of a hybrid outside the range of its parents; base
0.63, SFT 3.20 in this subset of 300 pairs), whereas the first 16 base
layers abolished the repair (0.38). In Apertus, the first 8 base layers
under SFT upper layers likewise left the repair intact (4.15), the first
12 removed most of it (1.33), and the first 16 all of it (−0.94);
conversely, the first 8 SFT layers under base upper layers produced part
of the repair (1.21) and the first 12 all of it (4.15). The repair thus
involved layers 9 to 16, with a partial contribution of the layers
below. To ask where in the prompt the repair acts, we exchanged the
internal states between the checkpoints at selected positions of the
prompt (activation patching; Figure 2D). Note that in the prompt for the
truth judgments the question precedes the statement, so that the
statement is read with the task known, and the positions after the
statement contain no question, only the instruction to answer with one
word and the answer cue (“Answer:”). At layer 16, the SFT model’s
states at the positions after the statement repaired the base model
completely (OLMo 2: 0.63 → 3.26; Apertus: −0.87 → 4.15), and the base
model’s states at these positions removed most or all of the repair in

blocks.en:
Patching at two layers cannot show where the repair first appears. We
therefore repeated the patching at 12 layers between 2 and 32, with 100
statement pairs (Figure 7C; the values are in the same summary file as
for authorship; on this subset, d′ = 0.34 for the OLMo 2 base model and
3.09 for its SFT model, and −0.86 and 3.64, the maximum for 100 pairs,
for Apertus). We express each effect as the share of the difference
between the two checkpoints that the patch transferred. The two models
differed. In OLMo 2, the repair appeared first at the statement
positions: The SFT model’s statement states alone transferred 22% of
the repair at layer 10, 82% at layer 12 (d′ = 2.59), and 67% at layer
14, although all layers above and all other positions were those of the
base model. The share then fell to 33% at layer 16 and to zero from
layer 20 onward. The positions after the statement showed the
complementary course (36% at layer 10, 37% at layer 12, 52% at layer
14, 97% at layer 16), and the final position alone carried the repair
only from layer 20 onward (89%). The reverse direction gave the same
picture: The base model’s statement states lowered the SFT model from
3.09 to 1.38 at layer 12 and to 1.75 at layer 14, and had little effect
at layer 16 (2.92) and none above. In OLMo 2, supervised fine-tuning
thus changed how the statement itself is represented at mid-depth, in a
way that the upper layers of the base model could read correctly; the
information then passed to the answer cue and to the final position. In
Apertus, in contrast, the SFT model’s statement states transferred at
most 23% (layers 12 and 14), whereas its states after the statement
transferred 46% at layer 6 and 96% at layer 10. In the reverse
direction, the base model’s states after the statement lowered the
Apertus SFT model progressively from layer 10 onward, and its statement
states did not lower it at any layer; note that the Apertus SFT model
was at the maximum d′, so that a small disruption would not be visible.
Hence, the two models agree in that the repair has reached the positions
after the statement by the middle of the network, but they differ in
where it arises: at the statement positions in OLMo 2, and at the answer
cue in Apertus.

blocks.en:
To see which of the two patterns is more typical, we ran the same sweep
for the two Gemma 3 models, comparing the base model with the final
post-trained model at 12 layers each. These models had not been
localized before, because their base models placed only 19% and 26% of
their probability on the two answer words (Section 2.8); the results
should be read with this in mind. Note also that the post-trained Gemma
3 12B, like the Apertus SFT model, was at the maximum d′, so that a
disruption of these models by base states cannot be measured unless it
is large. In both Gemma 3 models, the states after the statement carried
the repair completely from about half of the depth onward (Gemma 3 4B,
34 layers: 75% at layer 17 and 97% at layer 20; Gemma 3 12B, 48
layers: 100% from layer 20). Below that depth, other positions
contributed. In Gemma 3 4B, the post-trained model’s statement states
repaired the base model only slightly (at most 19% [15, 26], at
layer 11), whereas the base model’s statement states abolished the
repair in the post-trained model almost completely at layers 11 and 14
(d′ = 0.09 and 0.20, from 3.42). In Gemma 3 12B, the post-trained
model’s statement states transferred up to 45% [28, 77] of the
repair (layer 12), and at layer 16, one third of the depth, the repair
was carried mainly by the positions before the statement, i.e., by the
instruction and question (90% [63, 100], and still 30% [17,
49] at layer 20), when the positions after the statement transferred
only 9%.

blocks.en:
Across the four models, the states after the statement thus carried the
repair from about the middle of the network onward. Below that, the
share that the post-trained model’s statement states alone transferred
to the base model peaked at 82% [73, 91] in OLMo 2 (layer 12), 45%
[28, 77] in Gemma 3 12B (layer 12), 23% [20, 27] in Apertus
(layer 14), and 19% [15, 26] in Gemma 3 4B (layer 11). The
statement representation therefore contributed in all four models,
strongly in OLMo 2 and to a smaller, but reliable extent in the others;
in the reverse direction, which is informative only for OLMo 2 and Gemma
3 4B, the base model’s statement states removed about 60% and nearly
all of the repair, respectively. Note that a patch of the positions
after the statement at a given layer transfers everything that these
positions have gathered from the statement in the layers below; it shows
where the difference between the checkpoints sits at that layer, not
which computation produced it. Exchanging the statement states at all
layers up to a given depth at once would separate the two, and was not
done.

blocks.en:
Because the question precedes the statement in this prompt, we also
posed the judgment with the statement placed before the question. The
pattern of the answers was the same, and more pronounced: The base
models ordered the negated statements at or below chance (OLMo 2: d′ =
−0.14 [−0.24, −0.05]; Apertus: −2.13 [−2.29, −1.99]), and the
SFT models judged them nearly as with the default prompt (3.42 and
4.54). The repair by supervised fine-tuning thus does not depend on the
question being known when the statement is read. Patching across layers
with this prompt (same 12 layers, 100 statement pairs) gave the same
localization as with the default prompt. In OLMo 2, the SFT model’s
statement states alone transferred 36%, 75%, and 61% of the repair at
layers 10, 12, and 14 (base model: d′ = 0.85, 2.14, and 1.69, from
−0.36; SFT model 2.99), and the base model’s statement states lowered
the SFT model at the same layers (to 2.13, 1.25, and 1.71); the states
after the statement carried the repair completely from layer 16 onward
(3.09), and the question line by itself transferred nothing in either
direction. In Apertus, the SFT model’s statement states did not repair
the base model at any layer (at layers 8 to 12 they even lowered it, to
between −3.01 and −2.64, from −2.11), whereas its states after the
statement transferred the repair partly from layer 4 and completely from
layer 12 onward. Because the statement is read before the question in
this prompt, the contribution of the statement states in OLMo 2 cannot
reflect a reading of the statement in the light of the task: Supervised
fine-tuning changed how this model encodes a negated statement as such.

blocks.en:
Steering at the answer position was consistent with a readout that uses
the represented truth direction after SFT; as explained in Appendix D,
this is a consistency check rather than an independent test. Shifting
the internal state at the answer position along the direction that
separates true from false negated statements (±2 SD, layer 21; Appendix
D) moved the answers of both SFT models toward the correct answer, more
than the control directions (Apertus: +0.36 nats, p = .02; OLMo 2:
+1.07, p ≤ .04), and in these models the truth direction coincided with
the decision direction (cosine ≈ 1.0). In the base models, it did not
(Apertus: −0.14, p = .13–.33; OLMo 2: +0.09, p ≥ .54), although in both
base models the positive control, too, exceeded only the norm-matched
controls. Supervised fine-tuning thus aligned the answer with the
represented truth direction; whether the Apertus base model used this
direction with the wrong sign, as its negative sensitivity would
suggest, could not be established.

blocks.en:
In summary, the truth of negated statements could be decoded at ceiling
from the last prompt position before and after post-training, the
answers of several base models did not use this information, and
supervised fine-tuning repaired the answers, through weights in the
middle layers. In all four models in which we could trace the repair, it
resided at the positions after the statement from about the middle of
the network onward. Below that, the representation of the statement
itself carried most of it in OLMo 2 and a smaller part in the other
three models (19–45%), and in Gemma 3 12B the positions before the
statement carried it at one third of the depth. Note that the Gemma 3
base models answered with low answer probability, and that two base
models had nothing to repair.

blocks.en:
What do the training data teach? The direction of the change differed
between the judgments: Post-training impaired the readout of authorship,
repaired that of negated statements, and reshaped that of the reviews.
To examine whether this corresponds to the supervised fine-tuning data,
we searched the SFT mixtures of OLMo 2 and Apertus. Both contained
thousands of requests to judge statements as true or false (Tülu 3:
2,685; Apertus, extrapolated: about 2,300), largely factual claims in
Tülu 3 and mathematical statements with explicit reasoning, often
including negations, in Apertus. In contrast, we found no request to
judge whether a text had been written by a human or by an AI: The search
pattern matched five conversations in Tülu 3 and none in the Apertus
sample, and on inspection none of the five posed this judgment (they
concerned, e.g., a training script for an audio classifier and summaries
of research papers; the matches are listed in the repository). The
matches for fake or deceptive reviews were sentiment tasks or summaries
of research papers. Because our judgments were posed in German, we
repeated the search with German patterns in the conversations written in
German, which made up only 0.1% of Tülu 3 (992 conversations) and 1.7%
of the Apertus sample (6,330). They contained no request to judge
authorship and no deception judgment, two mentions of AI-generated text
(Apertus), and six true/false questions. Note that a search with regular
expressions can miss requests that are phrased differently, and that the
German subsets are so small that their search has little power. The
census is thus consistent with the idea that post-training improved the
one judgment for which the training data contain examples, where the
base model read it wrongly, and impaired or merely reshaped the
judgments for which we found none; on its own, it cannot establish this.

blocks.en:
Because the background condition C0 did not learn to answer with the two
answer words, whereas the three conditions with authorship examples did,
we compared each condition with three baselines: C0; C3, the condition
with random labels, which learned the question and the answer words but
no valid mapping; and C4, which practiced an unrelated judgment in the
same layout (differences in d′ with 95% CIs from a grouped bootstrap
that resamples texts and is conditional on the three seeds per
condition). Practicing the unrelated judgment left the authorship
answers where C0 left them (C4 − C0 between −0.13 and +0.10 on the three
test corpora, all CIs including zero; on the held-out news, C4 was
higher than C0, +0.34 [0.26, 0.43]), so that practice with a
judgment as such did not explain the effects of the authorship labels.
Note that the C4 models never answered “AI” (“KI”) in any run, so
that their d′ is a ranking of graded preferences under a saturated
criterion, and that C3 was unstable across seeds (criterion c between
−1.10 and +2.33). Two thousand correctly labeled judgments of news texts
sufficed to raise the sensitivity of the answers far above both
baselines, not only on held-out news but also on texts from other
generators and genres: the newspaper segments, written by GPT-5.4 (C1 −
C3: +2.23 [1.56, 3.17]; C1 − C4: +2.37 [1.74, 3.29]), and the
textbook summaries (+1.36 [1.11, 1.64]; +1.42 [1.15, 1.73]). On
the held-out news, C1 was at the maximum for both generators and all
text lengths (d′ = 3.8–4.0 are the ceilings of the subsets), so that
its success there was not due to recognizing one generator or one
length; the breakdown cannot exclude that the models detect the
generation procedure that the training and held-out texts share. The
information had been represented all along; a small amount of valid
training made the answer read it. On the short chats, however, the same
training made the answers worse than chance (−0.58), also relative to
random labels (C1 − C3: −0.36 [−0.69, −0.06]) and to the unrelated
judgment (C1 − C4: −0.62 [−1.01, −0.25]), because the properties
that distinguished generated from human news did not distinguish
generated from human chat messages in the same way.

blocks.en:
The stereotype acted according to its validity, but only partly
reliably. Measured with the formality score used for the labels, AI
texts were less formal than human texts in the chats and newspaper
segments (AUC = .40 [.32, .48] and .39 [.28, .49]) but more
formal in the textbook summaries (.70 [.65, .75]). Relative to
random labels, the stereotype improved the answers on the textbook
summaries (C2 − C3: +0.29 [0.11, 0.49]; C2 − C4: +0.35 [0.15,
0.57]) and lowered them on the newspaper segments, though not reliably
(−0.29 [−0.61, 0.07]; −0.15 [−0.57, 0.25]); on the chats, the
result depended on the baseline: The stereotype did not differ from
random labels (−0.08 [−0.39, 0.24]) and was lower than the unrelated
judgment, though not reliably (C2 − C4: −0.33 [−0.77, 0.08]),
because random labels themselves lowered the answers on the chats. Note
also that the stereotype labels were not independent of other text
properties: The more formal half contained more short texts, more texts
on business and domestic politics than on sports, and more texts from
Gemma 3 12B than from Qwen3 8B. Random labels lowered the answers
slightly on the chats relative to C0 (−0.26 [−0.52, 0.00]). Note
that the background condition did not reproduce the effect of the
official fine-tuning. The official SFT, which updated all weights on the
full mixture of about 940,000 conversations, lowered the sensitivity on
the newspaper segments and textbook summaries (d′ about −0.5) and
shifted the criterion strongly toward “human”; our background
condition, with 2% of the conversations, one epoch, and low-rank
adapters, left the judgments close to those of the base model. The
conditions therefore show that a training signal can set the direction
of the readout against a neutral background; they do not yet show that
the decline after the official fine-tuning has the same origin.
Fine-tuning with a larger share of the original mixture, or removing and
enriching specific parts of it (e.g., conversations in which the
assistant talks about AI), could identify which training data install
the misreading.

blocks.en:
Did the training change the representation of the texts or the way it is
read out? Probes trained within each fine-tuned model decoded authorship
at the last prompt position as well as in the base model (conditions C0
to C3; C4 was not included in this analysis; e.g., newspaper segments,
mean of layers 20 and 24, i.e., about two thirds of the depth: d′ = 3.14
in the base model vs. 2.93–3.14 after fine-tuning; chats: 1.42
vs. 1.32–1.45), and probes transferred between the base and the
fine-tuned models without loss at the text positions in every condition
(transfer deficit ≤ 0.02 d′, with one exception of 0.15 in the upper
layers for C1 on the textbook summaries; note that the probes for the
newspaper segments and textbook summaries were near their maximum). At
the last prompt position, in contrast, the deficit grew with depth, most
strongly after training with valid labels (upper third, newspaper
segments: C0 0.22, C1 2.09, C2 0.77, C3 0.86; textbook summaries: 0.25,
1.19, 0.72, 0.97). The training thus left the representation of the text
essentially unchanged, as far as the probes can tell, and reorganized
the position at which the answer is formed. That random labels also
reorganized this position, while barely changing the answers, shows that
what mattered for the answers was which readout was learned, not how
much the answer position changed. The chats illustrate this most
clearly: After training with valid news labels, the model represented
the authorship of the chats as well as before (probe d′ = 1.32) but
judged them below chance (−0.58), consistent with the reversed transfer
of news-trained probes to the chats (Section 3.1). The dissociation that
we observed after the original post-training was thus reproduced
experimentally, by training data whose cues were valid for one genre and
misleading for another.

blocks.en:
The account that the valid news labels installed a readout of the cues
of the news, which mislead on the chats, makes a prediction that can be
tested item by item (Section 2.9). We fitted a probe for authorship on
the held-out news in the base model, at the text positions, so that it
is defined independently of any fine-tuned readout, and applied it
unchanged to the chats (mean of layers 20 and 24). This news probe
separated the chats with the wrong sign (d′ = −0.44 [−0.70, −0.15]).
If training with valid news labels makes the answer follow what
distinguishes AI from human news, the answers of the C1 models to the
individual chats should follow the probe’s scores, and those of the
other conditions should not. This was the case. Across the 300 chats,
the answers of the C1 models correlated with the news-probe score
(Spearman ρ = .68 [.60, .73], mean of three seeds; within the human
messages .70, within the AI messages .63), whereas those of the control
conditions hardly did (C0: −.11; C3: .04; C4: −.12 [−.23, −.01]);
the difference between C1 and the random-label condition was .63 [.51,
.75]. Stereotype labels produced a weaker correlation (C2: .34 [.22,
.46]). With a news probe fitted on the 14 articles of the newspaper
segments, the pattern was the same but weaker (C1: .51; C3: .04), and
this probe did not separate the chats reliably in the base model (−0.11
[−0.36, 0.14]).

blocks.en:
Any classifier that has learned to tell AI from human news might agree
with the C1 models on the chats, whatever happens inside the models. We
therefore repeated the test with two classifiers that use no
activations, logistic regressions on word and on character n-grams of
the same held-out news. They, too, separated the chats with the wrong
sign (d′ = −0.53 [−0.80, −0.28] and −0.55 [−0.84, −0.27]), so
that the reversal between the genres is a property of the texts and not
of the model’s representation. Their scores also correlated with the
answers of the C1 models (ρ = .32 [.21, .42] and .43 [.33, .53])
and not with those of the random-label condition (.07 and .03), but
clearly less than the scores of the news probe. When both predictors
were entered together, the news probe kept its relation to the C1
answers (partial ρ = .63 [.54, .70] controlling for the word n-gram
score; .59 [.49, .67] controlling for the character n-gram score),
whereas the n-gram scores added little (.06 [−.06, .18] and .16
[.04, .28]). The C1 answers thus followed what the base model’s
representation of the text says about the authorship of news, beyond
what surface n-grams of the news predict.

At the last prompt position, we also compared the direction along which
the C1 models’ answers to the chats varied with the direction that
separated AI from human news in the same model. The result depended on
how the two directions were estimated: The cosine was .85 (range across
seeds .82–.87) between the difference of the class means and the
difference between chats with high and low dv, .50 (.41–.59) when the
answer direction was estimated by ridge regression, and .28–.36 when
the weight vector of the news probe was used in place of the class-mean
difference, compared with a bound of .43 for 95% of random directions
and values near zero for C3 and C4. Note also that this comparison is
partly circular, because the last position of a model that answers the
news correctly carries its decision. We therefore do not rest a
conclusion on it. The statistics of the item-level test were specified
in the analysis brief before it was run, which is not documented in the
repository, and the inversion of the chats was known at that time.
Within these limits, the results support the following reading:
Fine-tuning on valid labels made the answers follow the authorship
signal for news that the base model already represents, and the answers
to texts of another genre followed this signal also where it pointed the
wrong way. They do not show along which direction of the fine-tuned
model’s internal states this readout runs.

blocks.en: 4 Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论

blocks.en:
In the present study we used authorship judgments as a test case for the
question of whether post-training changes what a language model
represents or how it reads this representation out. Across six
open-weight base models and three corpora of German texts, the
information that distinguishes AI from human texts was readily
available, both in the texts themselves and in the models’ internal
representations, but the answers did not use it, and often ordered the
texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of these answers
on average (Δd′ = −0.34 across families; −0.29 across three prompt
wordings), with considerable variation between models, text types, and
prompts, and in the two models with stage-wise checkpoints the change
occurred during supervised fine-tuning. Post-training also changed how
strongly a stated base rate moved the log-odds of the answers, from less
than the change in prior odds to more in most models, although relative
to the larger spread of their log-odds this held less generally. Model
stitching implicated the weights of the early layers, with the caveat
that stitched hybrids produce effects of their own, and activation
patching across layers showed that, from the middle of the network
onward, the states at the positions after the text transferred the
change between checkpoints and the states of the text did not; in the
lower layers, the text states carried part of the change in Apertus and
none of it in OLMo 2, and the positions of the instruction before the
text carried part of it in both. A judgment on public data, the truth of
negated statements, showed the complementary case: The truth could be
decoded at or near ceiling in all six model families, the answers of
several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired the
answers while the probes stayed at or near ceiling. Sweeps over layers
in four models located this repair at the positions after the statement
from the middle of the network onward; below that, the representation of
the statement itself contributed in all four, strongly in OLMo 2 (up to
82% of the repair) and to a smaller extent in the others (19–45%). In
a training study, a small number of labeled examples shifted the readout
in the direction their labels implied, and the item-level answers on
another genre followed a probe for the authorship of the training texts
that was fitted in the base model, more closely than they followed
surface classifiers of the same texts. In short, post-training changed
how a judgment is read out of information that the models represent, in
a direction that depended on the judgment. The stronger statement, that
this change leaves the representation of the text untouched and resides
only in the positions that follow the text, held for the probes at the
text positions and, in the patching, for authorship in OLMo 2. In the
other cases, the representation of the text changed as well: in the
lower layers of Apertus for authorship, and below mid-depth for
negation, strongly in OLMo 2 and to a smaller extent in Apertus and the
two Gemma 3 models. What all cases share is that, by the middle of the
network, the change resided at the positions after the text. Note that
the localization rests on two models for authorship and on four models
from three families for negation, and that for the deceptive reviews
(Appendix C) it was inconclusive.

blocks.en: Relation to previous work
blocks.zh: 与以往工作的关系

blocks.en:
Our findings are consistent with the growing evidence that language
models represent more than they say (Burns et al., 2024 ; Hu & Levy, 2023 ; Orgad et al., 2025 ), including for authorship
(Ackerman & Panickssery, 2025 ; Y. Zhou et al., 2026 ). They add three points.
First, the dissociation is not only a gap but frequently an inverse
ordering. A miscalibrated decision threshold, which has been proposed as
the main source of probe–answer gaps (Villuri et al., 2026 ), shifts the criterion
in terms of signal detection theory; it can lower accuracy but cannot
produce sensitivity below chance. Reversed readouts of a discriminative
direction have been described for steering vectors (Torop et al., 2026 ); here, the inverse
ordering occurred in the graded preferences behind the models’
unmodified answers, and in two model families the class-mean difference
at the answer position carried this inverse ordering (Appendix D). Note,
however, that the cues themselves were specific to the corpus: A probe
trained on the newspaper segments separated the chats with the wrong
sign (Section 3.1). A judgment below chance therefore need not reflect
an inverted reading of a single authorship representation; it can also
reflect a fixed policy whose cues are valid for one kind of text and
invalid for another. Second, the decline is linked to post-training.
Interestingly, in the closest related study, post-training had the
opposite effect: It created rather than abolished the ability of a model
to recognize its own texts (Ackerman & Panickssery, 2025 ). Recognizing one’s
own output and judging whether an arbitrary text was written by an AI
are different tasks, and it is conceivable that post-training sharpens
the first while it distorts the second. Third, our results bear on the
superficial alignment hypothesis, according to which a model’s knowledge
is acquired during pretraining, whereas post-training mainly teaches it
which formats to use (Zhou et al., 2023 ). This hypothesis has been
supported by behavioral evidence (Lin et al., 2023 ) and by comparisons of
representations between base and post-trained models (Kissane et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Prakash et al., 2024 ; Waldis et al., 2026 ), and it has been
qualified by the observation that post-training gains continue to grow
with the amount of fine-tuning data (Raghavendra et al., 2024 ; see also
Vergara-Browne et al., 2026 ). To our knowledge,
it has not yet been tested with causal interventions across checkpoints.
Our results provide partial support for it: Probes transferred between
base and post-trained checkpoints at the text positions wherever this
test was not limited by ceiling effects, and from the middle of the
network onward the states of the text could be exchanged between
checkpoints without changing the judgment. Below mid-depth, however,
exchanging the text states did change the judgment in several cases
(Sections 3.4 and 3.6), so that the representation of the text was not
left intact throughout. Note, however, that the information available at
the answer position declined after post-training in some models (Gemma
3, OLMo 3 Think), so that the hypothesis holds for the representation of
the text rather than for the model as a whole. In another respect, our
results qualify it. The change was not superficial in the sense of
affecting only the final stages of processing or the output format; it
involved weights in the early layers and altered how the question takes
up the text, and it had substantive consequences for the quality of the
judgment. This is consistent with the observation that a property
tracked across the stages of post-training is shaped mainly during
supervised fine-tuning (Heidari et al., 2026 ).

blocks.en:
Our localization agrees with previous comparisons of base and
post-trained models in one respect and departs from them in another.
That, from mid-depth onward, the effect of post-training resided in the
positions after the text rather than in those of the text agrees with
model diffing and cache patching, in which much of what fine-tuning adds
was concentrated at chat-template and system-prompt tokens (Leong et
al., 2025 ; Loos & Eberle, 2026 ; Minder et al., 2026 ). Because our
prompts used no chat template, our results suggest that the relevant
positions are those at which the task is posed, whether in template
tokens or in a question phrased in natural language. In contrast, the
stitching results, which implicated the early layers for authorship and
the middle layers for negated statements, depart from the common picture
that fine-tuning mainly alters the upper layers (Merchant et al., 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; X. Zhou, 2026 ). It is compatible,
however, with evidence that changes in the late layers can depend on
altered earlier computation (Y. Zhou, 2026 ), that post-training
retunes routing mechanisms formed in pretraining (Gupta et al., 2026 ), and that task
representations formed early select later processing pathways
(Bigoulaeva et al., 2026 ). This
conclusion is tempered by the observation that stitched hybrids can
judge worse or better than both parents (Section 3.4), so that stitching
shows where the weights that carry the difference reside rather than
where the difference is computed; a control judgment far from chance
showed no such overshoot, so that stitching does not disturb the models
in general, but whether the overshoot is specific to the changed
judgment or to judgments near chance remains open. Note also that
stitching without an adapter at layer ℓ is equivalent to exchanging the
full residual stream at all positions at that layer, so that our
stitching and patching results are two views of one family of
interventions rather than independent tests. Steering at the answer
position does not add an independent test either, because it largely
restates the difference between the classes in the answers (Appendix D).
Two further cautions apply. A probe shows that information can be
decoded, not that the model uses it (Elazar et al., 2021 ; Hewitt & Liang, 2019 ); this is why we rest
the claim that post-training changed the readout on the stitching and
patching results rather than on the probes. Conversely, interventions
along a subspace can change the output through a pathway other than the
one the subspace was meant to capture (Makelov et al., 2023 ); our steering results
therefore show which way the answer pathway reads a direction, and we
compared them with control directions drawn from the same high-variance
subspace and with the decision direction, but they do not prove that the
model uses this direction under natural conditions.

The direction of the change depends on the training
signal
blocks.zh:
改变的方向取决于训练
信号

blocks.en:
Post-training impaired the readout of authorship on average, and
repaired the readout of negated statements in the base models that
misread them, whereas it hardly changed the judgments of statements on
diverse facts, for which the answers of the base models were already
close to what could be decoded. A common account of these outcomes
follows from the second lens in Figure 1. Post-training does not add
information to the representation; it installs a way of reading the
representation out. Whether this improves or impairs a judgment then
depends on whether the training signal specifies a valid way of reading
the question. For truth judgments, the supervised fine-tuning data of
both models with stage-wise checkpoints contained thousands of
statements to be judged as true or false; for authorship, we found none.
In terms of the lens model, post-training changes the weights of the
second lens, and these weights are valid only to the extent that the
training data contain valid examples. Two observations qualify this
account. First, the base models of Qwen3 and OLMo 3 already read negated
statements correctly, presumably because their pretraining data
contained instruction-like material; for them, post-training had nothing
to repair. Second, the account runs the risk of circularity: If the
presence of a valid training signal were inferred only from the
improvement of a judgment, it would explain every outcome and predict
none. The inspection of the training data provides an independent
measurement, but a correlational one that rests on two data mixtures and
on a pattern search with limited power; it cannot show which examples
produced the repair (the truth judgments themselves, or, for instance,
the many mathematical and reasoning tasks that teach a model to read a
question precisely).

blocks.en:
We therefore manipulated the training signal directly (Section 3.7).
Adding two thousand correctly labeled authorship judgments to otherwise
identical fine-tuning data improved the readout of texts whose cues
resembled those of the training texts and impaired it where they did
not, and the probes at the text positions changed little. On the chats,
the item-level answers followed a probe for the authorship of news that
was fitted in the base model, which turns the post-hoc explanation of
the inversion into a tested prediction; they followed it more closely
than they followed surface n-gram classifiers of the same news, which
suggests that fine-tuning made the answer read features that the base
model already represents. The training signal can thus set the direction
of the readout, as the account assumes. The training study does not
show, however, that the decline after the official fine-tuning of OLMo 2
has the same origin: Our background condition, with a small part of the
original data and low-rank adapters, did not reproduce this decline, and
identifying the parts of real post-training data that install a
misreading remains a task for future work. The deceptive reviews
(Appendix C) fit the account only loosely: Post-training removed a
polarity heuristic that the base models shared, without improving the
judgments.

blocks.en:
Sensitivity, criterion, and the stated base
rate

费率

blocks.en:
Signal detection theory was useful here in two ways. First, it separates
what a threshold can explain from what it cannot. Many of the models’
binary answers were constant, which by itself would suggest a
miscalibrated threshold; the graded preferences behind them, however,
were ordered inversely in several models, which no placement of the
criterion can produce. Second, the theory offers a reference point for a
manipulation of the response bias. An ideal observer in a stationary
environment who is told the proportion of signal trials shifts the
criterion by the change in prior log-odds and leaves the evidence for
each stimulus untouched. This is a reference and not a norm for every
situation: Where the environment changes, weighting a stated base rate
less, or sampling answers in proportion to their probability, can be
adequate. The qualitative prediction, that the answers should move with
the stated odds, holds in either case. Human observers typically adjust
less than this (Macmillan & Creelman, 2004 ; Phillips &
Edwards, 1966 ), and in
some tasks neglect stated base rates in favor of the individual case
(Kahneman & Tversky, 1973 ). The base models
behaved like conservative observers: Their log-odds shifted in the
correct direction, uniformly across texts, but by 6–51% of the
reference amount. After post-training, the log-odds shifted by more than
the reference amount in five of six model families, and by different
amounts for different texts, so that the stated share no longer acted as
a pure shift of the criterion. Speculatively, a post-trained model
treats a sentence about the share of AI texts less as prior information
to be combined with the evidence and more as a cue about the expected
answer. Two qualifications apply. The post-trained models gave more
extreme log-odds in general, to the texts as well as to the base rate,
and relative to the spread of their own judgments the weight of the base
rate increased in most, but not in all, models and wordings (Section
3.3). Moreover, the benchmark presupposes that the log-odds of the two
answer words are read as a posterior, which is an idealization for base
models that place only about half of their probability on these words.
Within these limits, the comparison shows that post-training changed not
only which texts receive more evidence for “AI”, but also how the
models combine this evidence with what the prompt states about the
situation, a second aspect of the readout.

blocks.en: What reads the text
blocks.zh: 内容

blocks.en:
What does it mean that the change resides at the positions after the
text? In a language model, the answer is produced from the state at the
last position of the prompt. Every position after the text, i.e., the
question, the cue for the answer, and the last position itself,
retrieves information from the text through attention at each layer and
transforms it through the feed-forward blocks. Post-training could
intervene at either step, by changing what is retrieved or by changing
what is made of it, and the stitching results suggest that both are
involved. Speculatively, a psychological description of such a change is
a different construal of the task. A model after post-training may
understand “written by a human” differently than its base model did,
much as a task set determines which features of a stimulus an observer
selects and how they are mapped onto a response. In accounts of biased
competition, a task set acts early, at the stage of selection, and not
only at a late decision stage (Desimone & Duncan, 1995 ). It is instructive to
see that the effect of post-training on the authorship judgments, too,
involved weights in the early layers, and positions as early as the
instruction that precedes the text. Note that our data do not single out
the question as the place of the change: Where we could separate the
tokens of the question from the cue for the answer and the last
position, the latter carried most of the difference (Sections 3.4 and
3.6).

blocks.en:
The sweeps over layers show that the positions after the text are not
the whole story. For the negated statements in Apertus, most of the
repair appeared at the positions after the statement (the answer
instruction and cue), as the picture of a changed reader suggests,
although the statement states carried a reliable part of it (up to
23%). In OLMo 2, most of it appeared in the states of the statement
itself at layers 10 to 14, and the upper layers of the base model read
these states correctly; here, supervised fine-tuning changed what is
read, and the reader of the base model was adequate. The same held when
the statement was placed before the question, so that it was processed
without the task being known: The change of the statement states in OLMo
2 is therefore a change in how this model encodes a negated statement as
such, not in how it reads the statement in the light of the question.
Why the two models differ is open. It is conceivable that the difference
reflects their post-training data, or the degree to which the base model
already encodes negation at the statement positions; our data do not
distinguish these possibilities.

blocks.en:
Why would human-oriented post-training impair the detection
of AI
text?
blocks.zh:
人性化的后期训练 为什么会妨碍检测
大赦国际
短信吗?

blocks.en:
Our data do not answer this question conclusively, but they constrain
the possible answers. The lens analysis of the chat messages (Appendix
B) showed what most post-trained models took as signs of AI authorship:
long words, adjectives, nouns, and text that is hard to read, i.e., a
formal and nominal style. In our corpus, this was the wrong way round:
The AI messages, written by current models instructed to sound like a
private group chat, were more verbal and lexically more diverse than the
students’ messages. Except for Qwen3, whose base model already weighted
these properties inversely (cross-validated G = −.53, after
post-training −.61), the base models used them less. One possible
explanation, which our data cannot test directly, is an outdated
stereotype of AI text: The picture of AI writing as formal, elaborate,
and impersonal fits the output of earlier assistant models and is
widespread in texts about AI, and current models that imitate a group
chat no longer fit it. If this explanation is correct, the error is a
moving target that changes with each generation of models. Two
alternatives are less consistent with our data. Familiarity with the
model’s own style would predict that text in a formal assistant register
is judged human, which is the opposite of what we observed, and removing
the surface markers that the students had identified as typical of AI
text did not change the models’ judgments. OLMo 2 does not fit the
picture either: After supervised fine-tuning, it weighted the same
properties in the opposite direction and judged the chats slightly
better than its base model. Note also that the lens analysis is
correlational and that many of the text properties are correlated with
each other; it shows which properties the answers follow, not which ones
cause them.

blocks.en: Implications
blocks.zh: 影响

blocks.en:
Three implications follow, each of which requires further testing.
First, the side effects of post-training can be localized, and possibly
repaired. A stitched model that combined the first eight layers of the
Apertus base model with all upper layers of the fine-tuned model
discriminated better than either parent, although such hybrids also
produce effects of their own (Section 3.4). Whether such hybrids retain
the intended effects of post-training, such as instruction following, is
an open question, and the approach is related to combining fine-tuned
weights by interpolation or averaging (Wortsman, Ilharco, Kim, et al., 2022 ; Wortsman, Ilharco,
Gadre, et al., 2022 ). Second,
knowing where a side effect arises makes it possible to protect the
affected components during fine-tuning or to correct them with small,
targeted interventions instead of broader training; in our training
study, two thousand examples sufficed to change the readout in either
direction. That such interventions are practical has been shown, albeit
with the opposite intention, for the refusal behavior that post-training
installs: Refusal is mediated by a single direction in the residual
stream, and removing this direction abolishes it (Arditi et al., 2024 ), and tools that
optimize such edits automatically remove refusals while changing the
model’s other outputs only minimally (Weidmann, 2025 ). Note, however, that
the same ease of editing that makes targeted corrections possible also
shows how fragile safety-related post-training can be. Third, and in our
view most important, post-training can change how a question is read
while the knowledge that the answer would require remains in the model.
The answer then no longer reflects what the model represents. In the
terms of memory research, the information is available but not
accessible (Tulving & Pearlstone, 1966 ); in the terms of
the second lens in Figure 1, the readout weights the internal cues as if
their validity were different from what it is, and post-training can
make this misweighting worse. Whether language models can access their
own internal states at all is the question of introspection, for which
they show some, but limited and unreliable, abilities (Binder et al., 2024 ; Gurnee et al., 2026 ; Kadavath et al., 2022 ; Lindsey, 2025 ). Our case is a
concrete and measurable instance of a model that represents something
but says something else, and it suggests that comparing the
representation at the question positions with the answer might be a
useful tool for auditing models, in the spirit of distinguishing the
presence of a feature from the behavior it supports (Templeton et al., 2024 ) and of examining
which representations a model can verbalize (Gurnee et al., 2026 ). From the
perspective of self-regulation, in which post-training is often seen as
a top-down control of the dispositions acquired in pretraining, our
results add a cautionary note: A top-down task set can bias perception
and not only correct a decision.

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en:
Several limitations qualify these conclusions. We studied models with 4
to 12 billion parameters, and the below-chance judgments might be weaker
or absent in larger models. We derived the sensitivity of the answers
from the graded log-odds of the two answer words; because the binary
answer hardly varied in most conditions, our d′ characterizes the
evidence on which the answer is based rather than the binary decisions
themselves. The information that the models failed to use was largely
lexical and stylistic, as shown by simple n-gram classifiers, so our
results concern the readout of ordinary cues rather than of any deep
representation of authorship. The stitching analyses and the patching
for authorship were restricted to two models, because stage-wise
checkpoints with a clear change were available for these two only. For
the negated statements, the patching across layers additionally included
the two Gemma 3 models, whose base models answer with low probability.
These analyses covered two corpora for authorship and used the plain
prompt format, because base models cannot be queried with a chat
template. The patching across layers was run for one authorship corpus
and with 100 statement pairs, which was what the available computing
time allowed. The two further judgments were studied with four to six
models, steering for them with two models each and on 300 items, and the
effects of post-training on the reviews were small; steering did not
explain them. Steering itself is limited in two ways: It tests whether a
direction is read more than arbitrary directions, which a partly aligned
direction can fail even if it contributes to the answer, and it did not
reveal the change during SFT for authorship, which rests on stitching
and patching. The training study used one base model, low-rank adapters,
and training texts from other generators and of another genre than the
test corpora, and its background condition did not reproduce the effect
of the original fine-tuning; the stereotype labels were moreover
correlated with text length, topic, and generator, a confound that we
noticed only after the training runs and that a stratified assignment of
the labels would avoid. The interventions were applied to partly
different combinations of models and corpora, because the analyses were
added step by step and not all could be repeated for every combination;
only Apertus on the textbook summaries was examined with steering,
stitching, and patching alike. The newspaper segments stem from only 14
articles, so that bootstrap intervals that resample articles are likely
too narrow for this corpus. The authorship judgments used German prompts
(the truth and review judgments used English ones); a paraphrased prompt
reproduced the decline, a prompt with the question before the text
reproduced it on average but not in every family, and we did not test
English prompts for authorship. Models from different developers also
differ in their post-training recipes, including distillation from
larger models, the emphasis on reasoning, and the share of human
preference data, and our design cannot separate these factors; they are
a plausible source of the heterogeneity between models and text types.
Labeled examples improved the judgments of base and post-trained models
alike without closing the gap between them; they show that a correctable
belief contributes to the failure, but not how much of it. Finally, we
defined the family of hypothesis tests for the post-training contrasts
after inspecting the full set of comparisons; we therefore report the
result under a stricter correction across all contrasts as well, which
left five of six decreases significant.
blocks.zh:

至120亿个参数,以下的判断可能较弱
或者在更大的模型中缺失。 我们发现了答案的灵敏度
从两个回答单词的分级日志; 因为二进制
我们的回答在大多数条件下几乎没有变化,

他们自己。 这些模型未能使用的信息主要是:

代表作者身份。 缝合分析和补丁
作者仅限于两种模式,因为阶段性
只有这两个检查站有明确的变动。 对于

两个Gemma 3模型,其基础模型以低概率回答.

这件案子太窄了 作者的判决使用了德语提示

blocks.en: Conclusion
blocks.zh: 结论

blocks.en:
Language models can represent what an answer would require and still
answer otherwise. For authorship, post-training impaired such a readout
on average, and for negated statements it repaired one: Models that
write like humans failed to recognize their own kind of text, not
because they lacked the information but because of how they read it out.
In both judgments, the change between checkpoints was carried by weights
in the middle or early layers and had reached the positions after the
text by the middle of the network; whether it arose there or in the
representation of the text differed between models. To know what a model
knows, it is therefore not enough to look at its answers; one has to
look at how the question is read. A training study showed that the
training data can set the direction of this readout with little change
at the text positions. Future studies with larger models may show how
general this mechanism is, which parts of real post-training data
install a misreading, and whether such side effects can be prevented
without giving up the benefits of post-training.
blocks.zh:
语言模型可以代表一个答案需要并且仍然
回答其他问题。 对于作者,训练后会妨碍这种阅读
平均来说,对于否定的报表,它修复了一个: 模式
写得像人类一样 无法识别自己的文字
因为他们缺乏信息 但因为他们如何读出来。
在两项判决中,检查站之间的变动都是以重量计算。
在中层或早期,并且已经到达位置
文字由网络中间; 无论是从那里还是从中产生的
不同模式对案文的表述有所不同。 知道什么是模特儿吗?
因此,仅仅看一看答案是不够的。
看看问题是如何解读的。 一项培训研究表明,
培训数据可以设定此读取方向, 几乎没有变化
在文本位置。 今后使用较大模型的研究可能表明如何
一般说来,这种机制是真正的培训后数据的哪些部分
安装错误读取,以及是否可以防止这种副作用
而不放弃后培训的好处。

This study combines concepts from the psychology of judgment with
methods from machine learning and interpretability research. The two
fields often describe the same idea with different words, and they
sometimes use the same word for different ideas. Table A1 lists the
correspondences that are relevant here, ordered by the two lenses of

that are used in both fields with different meanings and states how we
use them in this paper.

blocks.en: B Lens-model analyses
blocks.zh: B 透镜模型分析

blocks.en:
Method. For each judge, i.e., the answers of a checkpoint or the
out-of-fold scores of a probe on its representation, we computed the
components of the lens model equation (Karelaia & Hogarth, 2008 ; Tucker, 1964 ) from linear regressions of
the ground truth and of the judgments on a set of interpretable cues:
the environmental predictability R e , the consistency of
the judge R s , the matching index G (the correlation of
the two predictions), the unmodeled agreement C, and the achievement
r a , which decomposes as r a = G
R e R s + C √(1 − R_e²) √(1 − R_s²).
Because the regressions are fitted in sample, we also report
cross-validated R e , R s and G (10-fold,
grouped by source). For the short chats, the cues were 34 text
properties from five groups (length and lexical diversity, readability,
syntax, cohesion, and word frequency) and properties that the students
had named as typical of AI text (e.g., dashes, capitalization), computed
with a feature extractor written for the lab course; for the reviews, 15
cues motivated by Ott et al.
( 2011 ), such as the rates of
first-person pronouns, of references to family and to the hotel or city,
of spatial details and of emotion words, and the length of the review
and of its words and sentences, all centered within the positive and the
negative reviews.

blocks.en:
Short chats. On the 300 messages for which probes were available,
the cues predicted authorship moderately well (R e = .56;
cross-validated .40). The answers of most post-trained models weighted
the cues in the direction opposite to their validity (cross-validated G:
Gemma 3 4B −.49, Gemma 3 12B −.58, Qwen3 −.61, Apertus after SFT −.57);
for Qwen3, this was already the case in the base model (−.53), whereas
the other base models were closer to zero (−.28 to −.04). The AI
messages in this corpus were richer in adverbs and verbs, lexically more
diverse, and contained longer sentences than the human messages (r = .16
to .23 with authorship), whereas the human messages contained more
adjectives, proper nouns, and long words; the post-trained models of
Gemma 3 12B, Qwen3, and Apertus took long words, adjectives, nouns, and
low readability as signs of AI authorship (e.g., Gemma 3 12B, mean word
length: r = −.04 before and +.24 after post-training; adjectives: −.06
and +.27). OLMo 2 showed the opposite weighting after SFT (G = +.37).
Probes weighted the cues in line with their validity in every checkpoint
(cross-validated G = .69–.78); because probes are trained on the ground
truth, this is expected by construction and only shows that the cues
were represented. In-sample values and the 422-message set including the
style-matched messages gave the same picture.

blocks.en:
Deceptive reviews. Fifteen cues predicted the ground truth
moderately well (R e = .56; cross-validated .55). Probes
again matched the environment closely in all 13 checkpoints of the four
models analyzed (G = .97–.99), as expected by construction. The answers
were poorly matched (G = .15–.83), and post-training changed this
matching in opposite directions: from .83 to .26 in Gemma 3 4B and from
.17 to .53 in Qwen3. After post-training, all models treated long,
detailed reviews as truthful, a cue without validity (r = .03 with the
ground truth), and ignored first-person pronouns, the most valid single
cue (r = −.33).

blocks.en:
Answers. All models judged the reviews close to chance (d′
between 0.00 and 0.86), although probes separated truthful from
deceptive reviews well (d′ = 2.5–3.0), at least as well as a classifier
on word frequencies (d′ = 2.44). Post-training changed the probes little
and the answers by small amounts in a direction that depended on the
model: Gemma 3 4B lost sensitivity (d′ 0.45 → 0.08), Qwen3 (0.06 → 0.50)
and Gemma 3 12B (0.52 → 0.86) gained, and the others changed little
(Table C1). What post-training changed consistently was a shared
heuristic. The base models judged positive reviews as more truthful than
negative ones, and review polarity accounted for 41–90% of the
variance of their judgments; post-training largely removed this
heuristic (2–32%), except in OLMo 3 Think (76%), and all final models
showed a strong bias toward “Truthful” (83–92% of the answers). The
localization and steering analyses were less conclusive than for the
other two judgments: Patching located the change at the question
positions in two of four cases, and steering did not explain it (see
below). The reviews are thus a case in which post-training reshaped the
readout without improving it.

blocks.en:
Convergence. Within each review polarity, the item-level
judgments of the five models post-trained mainly for conversation became
more similar: The mean correlation between models rose from .36 (range
.16–.50) for the base models to .52 (.45–.58) for the final models;
OLMo 3 Think did not join this convergence (.18–.33 with the other
final models). Without separating the polarities, the correlations fell
(from .75 to .48), because the shared polarity heuristic of the base
models disappeared.

(which lost sensitivity) and Qwen3 (which gained). In Qwen3, the gain
arose gradually over layers 2–18 in stitching; at layer 18, the base
model’s question states removed the gain from the final model (0.53 →
0.17; text states: 0.29), whereas the final model’s question states
raised the base model only partly (0.08 → 0.22; all positions: 0.49). In
Gemma 3 4B, the final model’s question states lowered the base model
(0.53 → 0.23; text states: no effect), but the base model’s states did
not restore the final model at any set of positions (≤ 0.25), and
stitching produced non-additive effects in the middle and upper layers
with strongly varying answer probability. Thus, the question positions
carried the change in two of the four directions tested.

blocks.en:
These results are less conclusive than those for authorship and negated
statements: The effects of post-training were small
(|Δd′| ≤ 0.44), their sign differed between models, and
neither localization nor steering explained them fully. We can only
speculate about the reason. Although judging whether a review is genuine
resembles judging whether a text was written by an AI on the surface,
the two differ in what the models bring to them: The cues that separate
truthful from deceptive reviews are subtle and specific to this corpus
(human readers, too, judge these reviews near chance (Ott et al., 2011 )), the models’ answers were
near chance before and after post-training, and we found no examples of
this judgment in the fine-tuning data. It is conceivable that
post-training is largely irrelevant to a judgment for which neither the
base model nor the training data provide a usable mapping from the
represented information to the answer; what it changed here was a
general heuristic (review polarity) and the response bias, not the use
of the valid cues.

D Steering at the answer
position

blocks.en:
The probes and the answers could dissociate either because the answers
ignore the authorship information or because they use it with the wrong
sign. As a check on the second possibility, we shifted a model’s
internal state at the position where the answer is produced along the
direction that separates AI from human texts (estimated on held-out
groups; Section 2.7), and measured how the answer changed. The primary
test used shifts of ±2 within-class standard deviations, which kept
48–77% of the shifted texts within the range of the observed texts (±1
SD: 60–94%). We compared the effect with 100 control directions per
cell, each drawn once and applied to all texts: 50 random directions
within the high-variance subspace of the activations and 50 differences
between random halves of the texts within each class. The controls took
either steps of the same length as the authorship direction
(norm-matched) or steps of two standard deviations along their own
direction (scale-matched), which kept them within the range of the texts
as often as the authorship direction (49–69%). As a positive control,
we shifted along the direction that the model’s own answers follow (the
decision direction). In 21 of 25 cells (model × corpus × layer,
including the truth judgments of Section 3.6 and the review judgments of
Appendix C), the decision direction moved the answer more than the
norm-matched controls (rank-based p ≤ .05), so that the test can detect
a direction that the answer reads; against the scale-matched controls,
this was the case in 16 of 25 cells. Where the positive control failed,
a null result for the authorship direction is not informative.

blocks.en:
In six of the 17 authorship cells, the authorship direction moved the
answer more than the controls (rank-based p ≤ .06 against both control
families; with 100 controls, the smallest possible p is .01, so that no
cell would survive a correction for 17 tests), and in all six it moved
it the wrong way: Shifting a text toward “AI” made the model answer
“human” more often. This was the case for the short chats in Gemma 3
12B (layer 31: −7.38 nats; rank-based p = .01 against both control
families), Gemma 3 4B (layer 17: −1.74; p = .04 norm-matched, .06
scale-matched), and Qwen3 (layers 24 and 30: −1.18 and −2.06; p ≤ .03),
and for the newspaper segments in Qwen3 (−0.43 and −0.85; p ≤ .04). In
these cells, the authorship direction pointed against the decision
direction (cosine −0.59 to −0.92), and the answers were clearly below
chance (Table 2). Note that these are the cells with the most negative
d′, and that this is expected: The authorship direction is the
difference between the class means at the position from which the answer
is read, so that, if the answer depends approximately linearly on this
state, shifting along it must reproduce the observed difference between
the classes. Across the 25 cells, the effect of a shift by one class
distance correlated with the observed difference (r = .91). The test
therefore does not provide evidence that is independent of the answers’
d′; it shows that the inverse ordering is carried by the class-mean
difference at the answer position, more than by typical directions. In
the remaining cells, the authorship direction did not move the answer
more than arbitrary directions: Gemma 3 4B on the newspaper segments
(−1.04 and −2.00 at layers 22 and 28; p = .26–.42), Apertus and OLMo 3
on the textbook summaries before and after SFT, and Gemma 3 12B on the
newspaper segments, on which its answers were at chance (+0.03). In some
of these cells, the positive control did not exceed the scale-matched
controls either (Gemma 3 12B on the newspaper segments, Gemma 3 4B at
layer 28, Apertus at layers 21 and 27 and OLMo 3 after SFT; Table D1),
so that their null results are weaker evidence. In the strongest cell
(Gemma 3 12B on the chats), the decision direction itself did not
clearly exceed the norm-matched controls (p = .069; scale-matched: p =
.01), and only 48% of the shifted texts stayed within the observed
range. The norm-matched controls in the subspace of leading components
moved the state far outside the observed range in the Gemma 3 and Qwen3
cells, so that the scale-matched controls are the fairer comparison. In
summary, where the answers ordered the texts inversely, the class-mean
difference at the answer position carried this inverse ordering;
steering at earlier layers or at the text positions, which would be an
independent test, was not carried out.

blocks.en:
A complementary, descriptive comparison concerns the size of the
effects. Shifting a text by one class-mean distance along the authorship
direction, i.e., from the average human text to the average AI text,
changed the answer in the same direction as the observed difference
between AI and human texts in all 16 cells in which the bootstrap
interval of this difference excluded zero, and in 23 of the 25 cells
overall (e.g., Qwen3 on the newspaper segments: −0.50 and −0.66 nats
vs. an observed difference of −0.59). As stated above, this agreement is
expected if the answer depends approximately linearly on the internal
state; it is consistent with the patching results (Section 3.4).

blocks.en:
Steering did not, however, reveal what post-training changes for
authorship. In the Apertus base model, shifting toward ‘‘AI’’ moved the
answer in the correct direction, increasingly so with depth (+0.08,
+0.21, and +0.35 nats at layers 16, 21, and 27), but not more than the
control directions (p ≥ .15), and after SFT the effect was close to zero
(−0.04 to +0.04). In OLMo 3 Think, neither the base nor the SFT model
used the direction (−0.01 and +0.09). 2 2 2 An earlier comparison, in
which the SFT model received its chat template and the base model the
plain prompt, had suggested a reversed use after SFT (−0.27); with the
same plain prompt for both checkpoints, this was not the case. The
change of the answers during SFT is therefore localized by the stitching
and patching analyses (Section 3.4), not by steering.

blocks.en:
Among the individual comparisons, six decreases survived Holm correction
within this family of 18 tests (all p_Holm ≤ .013): Gemma 3 12B (Δd′ =
−0.95 [−1.28, −0.66]), Qwen3 (−0.57 [−0.79, −0.36]), Gemma 3 4B
(−0.50 [−0.72, −0.29]), Apertus (−0.47 [−0.71, −0.25]) and OLMo
2 (−0.32 [−0.52, −0.12]) on the textbook summaries, and Qwen3 on the
newspaper segments (−0.65 [−0.93, −0.42]). On the short chats, three
decreases of similar size (Gemma 3 4B: −0.51; Apertus: −0.47; Gemma 3
12B: −0.45; uncorrected p ≤ .008) did not survive Holm correction
(p_Holm = .059–.074), because the chat estimates were less precise (61
independent originals compared with 119 pairs for the textbook
summaries); they remained significant under false-discovery-rate
control. Two increases were significant only without correction or under
false-discovery-rate control: OLMo 2 on the short chats (+0.35 [0.06,
0.63]) and OLMo 3 Think on the textbook summaries, the latter in a
condition with low answer probability. Note that we defined the family
of tests post hoc as the comparisons that address our hypothesis; Holm
correction across all 75 contrasts that we tested (of 129 computed),
including comparisons between adjacent post-training stages and across
prompt formats, left five of the six decreases significant. Note also
that three of the six decreases did not hold with another wording of the
prompt: For OLMo 2 on the textbook summaries, the change was +0.18 with
the paraphrased prompt, and for Qwen3 it was +0.10 on the textbook
summaries and +0.04 on the newspaper segments with the question placed
before the text (Section 3.2). Hence, post-training lowered the
sensitivity of the answers on average, but neither uniformly nor in a
single direction across models and text types.

blocks.en:
Sublayer types. Both sublayer types contributed. Exchanging only
the attention blocks or only the feed-forward (MLP) blocks of the first
8 Apertus layers had partial effects in both directions (e.g., restoring
the base model’s blocks under SFT: attention +0.17 [−0.06, 0.40],
MLP +0.18 [0.03, 0.37], both together +0.59). In OLMo 2, the base
model’s MLP blocks of the first 16 layers restored discrimination almost
completely (−0.09 [−0.29, 0.11]), whereas its attention blocks did
so only partly (−0.35 [−0.55, −0.19]). Within the limits just
described, the change thus appears to be distributed over the early
layers and to involve both attention and feed-forward blocks.

blocks.en:
Figure 9: Figure S2. Post-training changes the text positions
little and reorganizes the answer position. For each layer, a linear
probe was trained on one checkpoint and tested on the other (base
vs. final post-trained model, both directions averaged); the transfer
deficit is the loss in d′ relative to the probe trained on the
checkpoint itself. A deficit of 0 means that the same direction
separates the classes in both checkpoints. Dark lines: OLMo 2 7B (solid)
and Apertus 1.5 8B (dashed), the two models included in all six sets;
thin grey lines: the other models (OLMo 3 Think and Instruct, which
share a base model, counted separately); thick light line: mean over all
models at the text positions (authorship corpora only). At the text
positions, probes transferred with little loss at every depth (largest
deficit 0.54; on the chats, where they were well below ceiling, 0.16).
At the last prompt position, at which the answer is produced, the
deficit grew with depth in all models and tasks, although probes trained
on each checkpoint itself still decoded the information. For the negated
statements, the deficit drops to zero at mid-depth because both
checkpoints are at ceiling there (AUC = 1); OLMo 2 shows no deficit in
the upper layers for this set.
